It is usually a Windows or domain account that was deleted or renamed, since SQL Server will not let you drop a login that owns a job. The query in Step 2 lists every job whose owner has gone, and sp_update_job with @owner_login_name reassigns them.
post_title: SQL Agent Job Failed: Finding the Step That Actually Broke

question: Do I need to restart SQL Server after enabling Agent XPs?
answer: No. MS Docs states the setting takes effect immediately without a stop and restart, and value_in_use changing after RECONFIGURE is the proof. You may need to reconnect SSMS for Object Explorer to notice, which is not the same thing as restarting anything.
post_title: SQL Server Agent Will Not Start, or “Agent XPs Component Is Turned Off” (Error 15281)

question: Does enabling Agent XPs start the SQL Server Agent service?
answer: No, and this is the single most common misunderstanding on the subject. Agent XPs controls whether the Agent's extended stored procedures can be called, which is what SSMS uses to populate the node. It has no power to start a Windows service. The relationship only runs the other way: MS Docs notes that starting the Agent service from SSMS enables the procedures automatically. Starting it any other way does not.
post_title: SQL Server Agent Will Not Start, or “Agent XPs Component Is Turned Off” (Error 15281)

question: I ran the sp_configure fix and the Agent node is still greyed out. Why?
answer: Either the RECONFIGURE did not run, or you are fixing the wrong thing. Check value_in_use for Agent XPs: if it is still 0, the RECONFIGURE was missed. If it is 1, the setting is right and SSMS is simply holding a stale connection, so reconnect Object Explorer rather than refreshing it. If it is 1 and a fresh connection still shows nothing, run the service state query, because the service is not running and the node has nothing to show you.
post_title: SQL Server Agent Will Not Start, or “Agent XPs Component Is Turned Off” (Error 15281)

question: Is it safe to leave Agent XPs enabled?
answer: Yes, on any instance that actually uses the Agent, and leaving it off while the Agent runs buys you no security and costs you visibility. It belongs to the same family of surface area switches as xp_cmdshell and Database Mail XPs, but unlike xp_cmdshell it does not hand anybody a shell: it exposes the Agent's own procedures, which are already gated by the msdb Agent roles. The 2 to be careful with are the other 2, and Get Database Mail and xp_cmdshell reports where they are turned on across an estate.
post_title: SQL Server Agent Will Not Start, or “Agent XPs Component Is Turned Off” (Error 15281)

question: Jobs have vanished from the Agent node but the service is running. Where did they go?
answer: Jobs live in msdb, so check which msdb you are looking at before assuming they were deleted. An msdb restored from another instance, or a point in time before the jobs were created, takes the job list with it. Query msdb.dbo.sysjobs directly rather than trusting the tree, and if the list is genuinely short, the rebuild is a scripting job rather than a configuration one. Get SQL Agent Job Overview gives you the full inventory in one result set.
post_title: SQL Server Agent Will Not Start, or “Agent XPs Component Is Turned Off” (Error 15281)

question: Why is there no SQL Server Agent in my SQL Server Express instance?
answer: Because Express does not ship one. The edition feature table on MS Docs lists SQL Server Agent as supported on Enterprise, Standard and Web, and not supported on Express or Express with Advanced Services. SERVERPROPERTY('EngineEdition') returning 4 confirms the edition. See the Express section; the scheduling options are Windows Task Scheduler or a different edition.
post_title: SQL Server Agent Will Not Start, or “Agent XPs Component Is Turned Off” (Error 15281)

question: Do I need to stop SQL Server Agent first?
answer: Not to run the statement, but it helps. Agent holds connections to msdb, and those connections are part of what the ALTER is waiting on. Stopping Agent removes a reconnecting source of exactly the sessions you are trying to clear, which often lets a plain ENABLE_BROKER complete without forcing anything.
post_title: SQL Server: ALTER DATABASE SET ENABLE_BROKER Taking a Long Time (Fix)

question: How long should I wait before forcing it?
answer: There is no useful timeout, because it will wait indefinitely. The question is not how long it has run, it is whether it is genuinely blocked. Run the sys.dm_exec_requests check below. If it names a blocking session, you are waiting on something real and you can decide whether to wait it out. If it does not, forcing the change will not help either.
post_title: SQL Server: ALTER DATABASE SET ENABLE_BROKER Taking a Long Time (Fix)

question: Is WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE safe on a production database?
answer: It is predictable rather than safe. It disconnects every other session and rolls back their in-flight transactions, so the cost is whatever those sessions were doing. On msdb that is usually tolerable because the workload is Agent jobs and mail. On a user database in the middle of a batch it is not. The rollback also has to finish before the change applies, so a long transaction does not disappear instantly just because you killed it.
post_title: SQL Server: ALTER DATABASE SET ENABLE_BROKER Taking a Long Time (Fix)

question: The command completed. Why is Database Mail still not sending?
answer: Broker being enabled is a precondition, not the whole path. Check the mail queue itself and whether the Mail host is started, because a queue that stalled while broker was disabled does not always resume on its own. Service Broker Health and Database Mail Queue reads both in 1 pass.
post_title: SQL Server: ALTER DATABASE SET ENABLE_BROKER Taking a Long Time (Fix)

question: Will this survive the next failover?
answer: Only on the node you ran it against. msdb is per instance, so the fix has to be applied on every replica. If you have only fixed the active node, the next failover puts you back where you started.
post_title: SQL Server: ALTER DATABASE SET ENABLE_BROKER Taking a Long Time (Fix)

question: Can I get at the data without touching the database that is already there?
answer: Yes, and it is the option to prefer. Restore the file under a new name with WITH MOVE for each logical file, as in the example above. It costs disk space for a second copy and destroys nothing, so you find out whether the backup is good before deciding what to do with the existing database.
post_title: The Backup Set Holds a Backup of a Database Other Than the Existing Database (Error 3154)

question: How do I see what is really in the backup file?
answer: RESTORE HEADERONLY reads it without touching anything, and RESTORE FILELISTONLY gives you the logical file names for WITH MOVE. Both answer “is this the file I think it is” before you commit to anything.
post_title: The Backup Set Holds a Backup of a Database Other Than the Existing Database (Error 3154)

question: Is WITH REPLACE safe?
answer: It waives three checks, not one: the database-identity check that raised 3154, the check that the tail of the existing log has been backed up, and the check that the files being overwritten belong to this database. The tail-log one is the dangerous half, because committed work since the last log backup is destroyed without a further warning.
post_title: The Backup Set Holds a Backup of a Database Other Than the Existing Database (Error 3154)

question: The names match, so why does SQL Server think they are different databases?
answer: Lineage, not name. A database restored from another server, or dropped and recreated, carries a different family GUID even with an identical name. That is exactly what the check is for.
post_title: The Backup Set Holds a Backup of a Database Other Than the Existing Database (Error 3154)

question: Are Cumulative Updates really cumulative?
answer: Yes. The latest CU includes everything from all earlier CUs for that version, so a new server goes straight from RTM to the newest CU in one step. There is no need to chain updates.
post_title: SQL Server Builds: Complete Version List and Support Lifecycle

question: How current is this page?
answer: The data-checked date in the banner at the top is exact. The page is regenerated from Microsoft’s published build tables after each SQL Server patch release, normally within a few days of Patch Tuesday.
post_title: SQL Server Builds: Complete Version List and Support Lifecycle

question: How do I check which build my SQL Server is on?
answer: Run SELECT SERVERPROPERTY('ProductVersion') and match the result against the tables above. The version check post walks through the other places the build number shows up.
post_title: SQL Server Builds: Complete Version List and Support Lifecycle

question: My version is out of support. What are my options?
answer: Three realistic paths: upgrade to a supported version, buy Extended Security Updates where the program still runs (2014 and 2016 as of the data-checked date, 2012 has ended), or move the workload to Azure where ESUs are included. My upgrade readiness script is the place to start planning.
post_title: SQL Server Builds: Complete Version List and Support Lifecycle

question: What happened to Service Packs?
answer: Service Packs ended with SQL Server 2016 (SP3 was its last). From SQL Server 2017 onward, servicing is Cumulative Updates plus GDR security releases only.
post_title: SQL Server Builds: Complete Version List and Support Lifecycle

question: What is the difference between a CU and a GDR?
answer: A Cumulative Update contains every fix so far, functional and security. A GDR (General Distribution Release) contains security fixes only. Microsoft runs the two as separate trains: stay on GDR only if your change policy genuinely forbids CUs, otherwise take the CU train and get the bug fixes too.
post_title: SQL Server Builds: Complete Version List and Support Lifecycle

question: Bulk insert network share access denied. What do I grant?
answer: Decide first which identity reaches the share. With a SQL Server login it is the service account, so the share and the NTFS permissions underneath it both need that account, which means a virtual account cannot work because it does not exist on the file server. Move the service to a domain account or a gMSA and grant that. With a Windows login from a client machine you are in the double hop and the answer is Kerberos delegation, not permissions. Check auth_scheme in sys.dm_exec_connections first: if it says NTLM, delegation is impossible until the SPN is fixed.
post_title: Cannot Bulk Load, Access Is Denied (Error 4861): It Is the Service Account, Not You

question: Bulk insert says access denied but I can open the file. How?
answer: Because you did not open it. If your session connected with a SQL Server login, the file is opened by the SQL Server service account, and your own rights on the file never enter into it. The capture on this page is the same statement against the same file seconds apart: refused with 4861 on a SQL login, three rows loaded on a Windows login. Run SELECT service_account FROM sys.dm_server_services and check that account's access, not yours.
post_title: Cannot Bulk Load, Access Is Denied (Error 4861): It Is the Service Account, Not You

question: Can I avoid the whole problem by using a format file or a different tool?
answer: A format file does not change anything, it is read by the same account and will fail the same way if it sits in the same folder. bcp is genuinely different, and it is the one workaround worth knowing: it is a client program, so it opens the file itself as whoever launched it and hands the rows to SQL Server over the connection. On the lab, with the service account holding no access at all to the import folder, bcp... in loaded the same file successfully both on a trusted connection and on the same SQL login that BULK INSERT had just refused. The trade is that the data travels over the client connection instead of being read in process, which is slower on large files, and the job now depends on the Windows account the scheduled task runs as.
post_title: Cannot Bulk Load, Access Is Denied (Error 4861): It Is the Service Account, Not You

question: Do I need bulkadmin as well, and what does it cost me?
answer: Yes, you need ADMINISTER BULK OPERATIONS or membership of bulkadmin, and its absence is a different error: Msg 4834, "You do not have permission to use the bulk load statement", with no path in it at all. That is how you tell a permission problem inside SQL Server from a permission problem in Windows. The cost is real: on the lab a login with bulkadmin, no sysadmin, read C:\Windows\win.ini through OPENROWSET(BULK...). The role grants the ability to read any file the service account can read, so treat it as a sensitive grant and review who holds it.
post_title: Cannot Bulk Load, Access Is Denied (Error 4861): It Is the Service Account, Not You

question: I granted the service account and it still fails. What did I miss?
answer: Check in this order. Did the entry reach the file, or only the folder, which is what icacls "C:\Imports\sales.csv" answers in one line. Is the path a folder rather than a file, which returns access denied even when permissions are perfect. Is the folder on a share, where NTFS and share permissions are two separate lists and the stricter one wins. And is the account you granted the one sys.dm_server_services named, rather than the Agent account, which is a different service.
post_title: Cannot Bulk Load, Access Is Denied (Error 4861): It Is the Service Account, Not You

question: OPENROWSET bulk operating system error code 5. Why do I not get one?
answer: You will not. OPENROWSET(BULK...) raised 4860 for the same permission fault that gave BULK INSERT a 4861 with operating system error 5, and 4860 carries no operating system code at all, only "does not exist or you don't have file access rights". If you need the code, point a throwaway BULK INSERT at the same path and read the number out of its message instead.
post_title: Cannot Bulk Load, Access Is Denied (Error 4861): It Is the Service Account, Not You

question: Which account does bulk insert use?
answer: One of two. On a SQL Server login it is the SQL Server Database Engine service account, named in sys.dm_server_services, which on a default modern install is the virtual account NT Service\MSSQLSERVER. On a Windows login it is you, impersonated, which works for a local path and needs Kerberos delegation for a UNC path from a third machine. If the statement runs in an Agent job step, check the step: a proxy or a SQL login connection in the step changes the answer again.
post_title: Cannot Bulk Load, Access Is Denied (Error 4861): It Is the Service Account, Not You

question: Is TRUSTWORTHY involved?
answer: Sometimes, but treat it separately. A database that relies on EXECUTE AS reaching outside itself needs either TRUSTWORTHY ON (broad, discouraged) or module signing (narrow, preferred). If your 15517 appeared after a restore, fix the owner first; TRUSTWORTHY resets to OFF when the backup is restored as a new database or after the original was dropped (measured on SQL Server 2025: ON before the backup, OFF after the restore), while a RESTORE WITH REPLACE over the same database kept it ON in the same test, so check is_trustworthy_on rather than assuming. Either way it is its own follow-up decision, not an automatic switch to flip.
post_title: Cannot Execute As the Database Principal (Error 15517)

question: The principal exists and I still get 15517. What now?
answer: Permission. The caller needs IMPERSONATE on the target user (or the target must be in a scope the caller can impersonate). Measured on SQL Server 2025: the message for a permission failure is identical to the missing-principal one, including the words "does not exist". GRANT IMPERSONATE ON USER::target TO caller; is the narrow fix.
post_title: Cannot Execute As the Database Principal (Error 15517)

question: Which features hit this beyond EXECUTE AS in procedures?
answer: Anything that impersonates a database principal on your behalf: Service Broker queue activation, DDL and DML triggers with EXECUTE AS, cross-database ownership chains relying on the owner mapping, and jobs that run in a database context. The restore-orphaned owner breaks all of them the same way.
post_title: Cannot Execute As the Database Principal (Error 15517)

question: Why does it say dbo does not exist? dbo always exists.
answer: The user dbo exists; the login it maps to does not. dbo is a mapping to the database owner’s SID, and when that SID matches no login on the instance, impersonating dbo has no identity to resolve to. Fix the owner, not the user.
post_title: Cannot Execute As the Database Principal (Error 15517)

question: Did any rows get inserted before it failed?
answer: For a single statement, no. The statement is terminated and the whole thing rolls back, so you do not get a partial row. A multi-row VALUES list is still one statement, so the same applies: all of it or none of it.
post_title: Cannot Insert the Value NULL Into Column (Error 515)

question: It is an ORM or an application doing the insert.
answer: Then cause one is far more likely than cause two, because those layers usually send every column. Something in the object is null where the column is not nullable. The message names the column, which maps back to the property.
post_title: Cannot Insert the Value NULL Into Column (Error 515)

question: Should I just make the column nullable?
answer: Only if it genuinely is optional. NOT NULL is a rule someone wrote down on purpose, and dropping it to clear an error pushes the problem into the data, where it becomes harder to find. Fix the insert first and change the schema only if the rule was wrong.
post_title: Cannot Insert the Value NULL Into Column (Error 515)

question: The message names a column I did not touch.
answer: Then you probably left it out. Omitting a NOT NULL column with no default gives the same message as inserting NULL into it. Compare the named column against your column list first, before looking at the data.
post_title: Cannot Insert the Value NULL Into Column (Error 515)

question: Why does my default constraint not work?
answer: Because you are passing the column explicitly with a NULL value. A default only applies when the column is absent from the statement. Verified on SQL Server 2025: with a default in place, omitting the column succeeded and passing NULL still raised 515.
post_title: Cannot Insert the Value NULL Into Column (Error 515)

question: Can a SELECT cause this, or only writes?
answer: A SELECT can. Shared locks still come out of the same pool, and MS Docs notes in Resolve blocking problems caused by lock escalation that a bookmark lookup with a PREFETCH clause raises part of a read-committed query to repeatable read, which can take many thousands of key locks on a statement that looks harmless. That is the same mechanism that makes an unselective index a lock escalation problem rather than only a performance one. If a read is the thing producing 1204, the index is usually the real answer: Get Lock Escalation, Contention Analysis, and Blocking Chains with Plan shows which statement and which plan.
post_title: SQL Server Cannot Obtain a LOCK Resource at This Time (Error 1204)

question: Do I have to restart SQL Server to change locks?
answer: Yes, and this is the one part of the fix that cannot be worked around. MS Docs states the server must be restarted before the setting takes effect, and you can see it in sys.configurations: value changes the moment RECONFIGURE runs, value_in_use does not change until the instance comes back. Because of that, get through the incident by batching the statement and schedule the restart properly.
post_title: SQL Server Cannot Obtain a LOCK Resource at This Time (Error 1204)

question: I got 1204 and locks is already 0. What now?
answer: Then the ceiling is memory, not configuration. The lock manager is capped at 60 percent of the Database Engine's memory, so look at the OBJECTSTORE_LOCK_MANAGER clerk and at what else on the instance is large. In practice there are 2 realistic causes: lock escalation has been switched off somewhere, by a table set to DISABLE or trace flag 1211 or 1224, or max server memory is set low enough that 60 percent of it is not much. Escalation is the first thing to check, because an instance with escalation working will normally convert a runaway statement to a table lock long before the lock manager fills.
post_title: SQL Server Cannot Obtain a LOCK Resource at This Time (Error 1204)

question: Is this the same as a deadlock, or as a lock timeout?
answer: No, and the 3 are worth keeping apart because the fixes are different. A deadlock victim gets Msg 1205 and SQL Server chose to kill your session to break a cycle. A lock request timeout gets Msg 1222 and you waited too long for a lock somebody else held. Error 1204 is neither: nobody was blocking you and nothing was waiting, the lock manager simply had no structure left to record your next lock. Nothing about reducing contention will help, which is why the message's suggestion to rerun with fewer active users is misleading here.
post_title: SQL Server Cannot Obtain a LOCK Resource at This Time (Error 1204)

question: Should I just raise locks to a bigger number?
answer: No. Set it to 0 and let SQL Server manage the pool, which is what MS Docs recommends. Raising a fixed ceiling trades 1 arbitrary number for a slightly larger arbitrary number, and the reproduction behind this page shows why you cannot calculate a safe one: a setting of 5000 gave out between 3,000 and 3,500 rows, because the pool is shared with every other session and with the page, object and owner structures. The option is also marked for removal in a future version of SQL Server, so any value you pick now is temporary by design.
post_title: SQL Server Cannot Obtain a LOCK Resource at This Time (Error 1204)

question: The message says to rerun when there are fewer active users. Does waiting help?
answer: Only if the cause really is other people. That is the case where a long-running transaction elsewhere is sitting on a large number of locks and the pool recovers when it finishes, and the per-session lock count will show it as 1 session holding most of them. If the count shows your own statement at the top, or if the ERRORLOG says static allocation, waiting changes nothing and the statement will fail at the same point every time you try it.
post_title: SQL Server Cannot Obtain a LOCK Resource at This Time (Error 1204)

question: Does a RESTORE throw this too, or is it only backups?
answer: Both, and the state number tells you which side you are on. Reproduced against a path that does not exist: a BACKUP returns Msg 3201, Level 16, State 1 and a RESTORE HEADERONLY returns Msg 3201, Level 16, State 2, each followed by Msg 3013 saying the operation is terminating abnormally. The 3013 is noise, the 3201 is the error. The difference that matters operationally is the permission being tested: on backup the service account needs to write to that folder, on restore it needs to read the file. A share that a backup job can write to is not automatically one a restore can read from, which is why restores fail on paths that have been backing up happily for months.
post_title: Cannot Open Backup Device: Operating System Error 5 (Access Is Denied)

question: It worked yesterday and fails today.
answer: Three usual culprits: the service account password changed or the account locked, antivirus started scanning the backup folder (operating system error 32), or the share was recreated, which resets share permissions even when NTFS permissions survive.
post_title: Cannot Open Backup Device: Operating System Error 5 (Access Is Denied)

question: The path works when I test it, so why does the backup fail?
answer: Because the backup does not run as you. SQL Server writes as its service account, so your own access to the folder proves nothing. sys.dm_server_services tells you which account is actually being refused.
post_title: Cannot Open Backup Device: Operating System Error 5 (Access Is Denied)

question: Why can I not back up to a mapped drive?
answer: Mapped drives belong to a user session and SQL Server does not have yours. The drive letter does not exist for the service, which is why you get operating system error 2 or 3 rather than 5. Always use the UNC path.
post_title: Cannot Open Backup Device: Operating System Error 5 (Access Is Denied)

question: Everyone started getting 4060 at once.
answer: Stop looking at logins. Something happened to the database. A database left in SINGLE_USER after maintenance is the classic version, and it locks out everyone except whoever holds the one connection.
post_title: Cannot Open Database Requested by the Login (Errors 4060 and 4064)

question: I am locked out of SSMS entirely.
answer: That is 4064, the default database one. On the connection dialog use Options, Connection Properties, Connect to database and type master. Then run ALTER LOGIN... WITH DEFAULT_DATABASE = [master].
post_title: Cannot Open Database Requested by the Login (Errors 4060 and 4064)

question: Is this a password problem?
answer: No. Authentication already succeeded. Both errors report as "login failed" and neither involves the password. The database is the problem, not the login.
post_title: Cannot Open Database Requested by the Login (Errors 4060 and 4064)

question: It works in SSMS but the application gets 4060.
answer: The application is asking for a different database, or asking as a different login. Read the database name inside the message and check it against sys.databases on that server: renamed, dropped, offline and restoring all produce this. If the name is right, the application's login has no user in it, and the error log reason line names both the login and the database.
post_title: Cannot Open Database Requested by the Login (Errors 4060 and 4064)

question: Can I just copy master.mdf from another server?
answer: No. Master holds the instance's own identity, logins, and configuration, and is tied to the build. A master from a different server or a different patch level will not start, and may leave you worse off than the damaged one you still had.
post_title: Cannot Recover the Master Database (Error 3417) and What the Log Actually Says

question: Does an 824 on database ID 1 mean the whole instance is lost?
answer: It means master is damaged, which stops the instance from starting, but it does not mean your user databases are affected. They are separate files and are usually intact. Recovering master gets the instance back and the user databases come with it.
post_title: Cannot Recover the Master Database (Error 3417) and What the Log Actually Says

question: How do I practise this safely?
answer: A container. Everything on this page was reproduced in a throwaway SQL Server 2022 container: damage the file, start it, read the log, put a good copy back, watch it come up. That last step is the one worth rehearsing, because it is the one you will be doing under pressure.
post_title: Cannot Recover the Master Database (Error 3417) and What the Log Actually Says

question: I searched 3417 and found nothing useful. Why?
answer: Because 3417 tells you the outcome, not the cause. Across 4 different kinds of deliberate master damage it did not appear at all, and a more specific error did every time: 5172 for a destroyed header, 824 for page or log corruption, 5120 for a permissions problem. Search the error above it in the log.
post_title: Cannot Recover the Master Database (Error 3417) and What the Log Actually Says

question: It happened straight after installing a Cumulative Update. Is master corrupt?
answer: Probably not. Every CU ships T-SQL upgrade scripts that run on the first start after the binaries are replaced. If they fail, Setup reports "Wait on Database Engine recovery handle failed" and the error log carries 912 and then 3417. The messages immediately before the 912 name the real cause. Microsoft's CU troubleshooting page walks that log, and the 3417 reference says the same thing this whole page does: the error is preceded by other errors, and those are the ones to read.
post_title: Cannot Recover the Master Database (Error 3417) and What the Log Actually Says

question: Should I be backing up master?
answer: Yes, and it is cheap. Master is a few megabytes and changes only when logins, jobs or server settings change. Without a backup, your recovery options reduce to file-level copies or a rebuild that discards every login and job on the instance.
post_title: Cannot Recover the Master Database (Error 3417) and What the Log Actually Says

question: The instance will not start after we moved the data files. Is it corruption?
answer: Almost certainly not. Look for FCB::Open failed and operating system error 5 in the log, which is a permissions problem on the file or the folder. Reproduced here by accident, because copying files back into place as the wrong user is exactly how it happens for real.
post_title: Cannot Recover the Master Database (Error 3417) and What the Log Actually Says

question: Does COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT change how my data is stored?
answer: No. It affects only the evaluation of that expression, for that statement. Nothing is written, no column definition changes, and the plan is the only thing that differs.
post_title: Cannot Resolve the Collation Conflict (Error 468)

question: Is 468 a sign something is corrupt or misconfigured?
answer: No. Every object involved is valid. Two of them store text under different rules, which is a design consequence of how the databases were created or restored, not a fault. The instance is healthy and the error is doing its job.
post_title: Cannot Resolve the Collation Conflict (Error 468)

question: Should I just standardise every database on one collation?
answer: It is the real fix if you own the estate and can afford it, and it is a migration rather than an afternoon: the database collation and every existing character column both have to change, and code that relied on case sensitivity has to be retested. Until that is scheduled, COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT at the comparison is the correct answer rather than a workaround.
post_title: Cannot Resolve the Collation Conflict (Error 468)

question: Why does a query that only touches one database still raise it?
answer: A temp table. #temp columns take tempdb's collation, which follows the instance, so joining a temp table back to a user database with a different collation compares two collations without ever naming a second database. Declaring the column COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT in the CREATE TABLE removes it.
post_title: Cannot Resolve the Collation Conflict (Error 468)

question: Why does the same query work in one environment and fail in another?
answer: Because collation follows the database, and a database keeps the collation it was created or restored with. Dev, test and production frequently differ for no better reason than which server default applied on the day each was built. That is also why 468 tends to appear first in whichever environment was restored most recently.
post_title: Cannot Resolve the Collation Conflict (Error 468)

question: Will this slow the query down?
answer: It can, if you collate the indexed column, because applying it to a column makes the predicate non-sargable and costs the seek. Put COLLATE on the other side of the comparison where you have a choice. Collating a temp table column at declaration avoids the question entirely.
post_title: Cannot Resolve the Collation Conflict (Error 468)

question: Can I make INSERT... EXEC ignore the extra columns?
answer: No. The shapes must match. If you only want some of the columns, capture the full result set into a staging table that matches the procedure, then select the columns you want out of it.
post_title: Column Name or Number of Supplied Values Does Not Match (Error 213)

question: Does an identity column count?
answer: No, and it trips people the other way. A bare INSERT... VALUES skips the identity column and expects a value for every other column; measured on SQL Server 2025, and the INSERT reference says the next identity value is simply used. Supply a value for it and you get Msg 8101, not 213. Where identity does bite is the count: a table of identity plus 2 columns given 1 value is still a 213. Name your columns and neither problem arises.
post_title: Column Name or Number of Supplied Values Does Not Match (Error 213)

question: My INSERT... EXEC used to work and now it does not.
answer: The procedure's result set changed, most likely after an upgrade or a patch. System procedures do this between versions. Run the procedure on its own, count the columns it actually returns now, and rebuild the target table to match.
post_title: Column Name or Number of Supplied Values Does Not Match (Error 213)

question: Why did TRY/CATCH not catch this?
answer: Because a static INSERT with the wrong column count fails at compile time, before the batch runs, so there is no runtime error to catch and the batch aborts. Verified on SQL Server 2025. Wrap it in sp_executesql and it compiles separately, at which point it is catchable.
post_title: Column Name or Number of Supplied Values Does Not Match (Error 213)

question: Why does the message not tell me which column?
answer: Because at the point it fails, SQL Server is comparing two shapes rather than validating a value. It knows the counts do not line up; it has no single column to blame. Compare your column list with sys.columns for the table and the mismatch is usually obvious.
post_title: Column Name or Number of Supplied Values Does Not Match (Error 213)

question: I added a WHERE clause to filter out the bad rows and it still fails.
answer: There is no guaranteed evaluation order. The optimiser may compute the conversion before the filter, so a query can work for months and then fail after a plan change with no deployment to blame. Use TRY_CONVERT, which cannot raise.
post_title: Conversion Failed When Converting the varchar Value to Data Type int (Error 245)

question: Is ISNUMERIC good enough for the check?
answer: No. ISNUMERIC returns 1 for 1e5, 1.5, $10 and 1,000, none of which convert to int. It answers a different question from the one you have.
post_title: Conversion Failed When Converting the varchar Value to Data Type int (Error 245)

question: The message names a value like 'not entered' that is nowhere in my query.
answer: That is the proof of what went wrong. The value comes from the column, not from your literal: SQL Server converted the column side to int and stopped at the first row it could not convert, which is why the failing value reads like data rather than code. The TRY_CONVERT... IS NULL query above lists every such row, and quoting the literal stops the column being converted at all.
post_title: Conversion Failed When Converting the varchar Value to Data Type int (Error 245)

question: Why is SQL Server converting the column and not my value?
answer: Data type precedence. int outranks varchar, so the column side converts, not the literal. Quoting the literal stops the conversion, and usually makes the query faster by keeping the predicate sargable.
post_title: Conversion Failed When Converting the varchar Value to Data Type int (Error 245)

question: My application hit this, not a person. Same fix?
answer: Same fix, applied to the login in the application’s connection string. Find the login name in the error output or the connection string, then use the smallest grant that fits what the application genuinely needs to do at runtime rather than what its installer needed once.
post_title: CREATE DATABASE Permission Denied (Error 262)

question: The catalog says severity 16, but my error shows Level 14. Which is right?
answer: Both, oddly. The message template sits in sys.messages with severity 16, but when the engine raises 262 it arrives at Level 14, the severity band SQL Server uses for permission errors. Measured on SQL Server 2025 for both the CREATE DATABASE and CREATE TABLE variants while writing this.
post_title: CREATE DATABASE Permission Denied (Error 262)

question: Which should I ask for: CREATE ANY DATABASE, dbcreator, or sysadmin?
answer: Ask for the smallest one that covers the job. A process that only creates databases wants CREATE ANY DATABASE. A person who also restores and drops what they create wants dbcreator, granted in the knowledge that it covers every database on the instance. sysadmin is not a fix for a missing create permission; it is a different job description.
post_title: CREATE DATABASE Permission Denied (Error 262)

question: Why does it say master when I never touched master?
answer: Because CREATE DATABASE is a server-level operation and the permission for it lives in master. The message names the database where the check failed, which is not necessarily the one your session was using.
post_title: CREATE DATABASE Permission Denied (Error 262)

question: Does the same thing happen when attaching a database?
answer: Yes, the message says “open or create” for exactly that reason. Files copied in from another machine or restored by backup tooling often arrive owned by whoever copied them, and the engine cannot open what it cannot read. Same account, same grant, same fix.
post_title: CREATE FILE Encountered Operating System Error (Error 5123)

question: I am an administrator on the machine. Why am I denied?
answer: Because the file is not created under your token. Your session asked SQL Server, and SQL Server’s service account asked Windows. It is the service account that was refused, and it is the service account that needs the grant.
post_title: CREATE FILE Encountered Operating System Error (Error 5123)

question: It works in the default data directory but fails on my D: folder. Why?
answer: Setup grants the service account full rights on the default directories at install time. Any folder you create afterwards starts with whatever it inherited, which usually does not include the SQL Server service. The icacls grant above is the missing step.
post_title: CREATE FILE Encountered Operating System Error (Error 5123)

question: What does operating system error 3 mean instead of 5?
answer: Path not found, and it usually arrives on 5133 rather than 5123 because the engine never got as far as the file: the folder in the FILENAME does not exist from the service’s point of view. Check for typos first, then for the difference between your drive mappings and what the service session can see, because a mapped drive letter that exists for you frequently does not exist for a service.
post_title: CREATE FILE Encountered Operating System Error (Error 5123)

question: Can this happen to tempdb or master?
answer: The system databases play by harsher rules: if master cannot open, the instance does not start at all, and tempdb is recreated at startup so a bad tempdb path also stops the service. 945 as a running-instance message is a user database story.
post_title: Database in Recovery Pending: Cannot Be Opened (SQL Server Error 945)

question: Is RECOVERY_PENDING the same as SUSPECT?
answer: No, and the difference decides how worried to be. RECOVERY_PENDING means recovery has not started because a file cannot be opened; fix the file and the database usually comes back untouched. SUSPECT means recovery ran and failed, which is a genuinely harder situation. 945 belongs to the first world.
post_title: Database in Recovery Pending: Cannot Be Opened (SQL Server Error 945)

question: The message mentions memory and disk space, but my disk is fine. Why say it?
answer: The message text covers every reason the open can fail and cannot know which one applied. The error log can: it records the specific operating system error, and in the reproduction for this post that was error 2, file not found. Read the log before acting on any of the three causes.
post_title: Database in Recovery Pending: Cannot Be Opened (SQL Server Error 945)

question: Why does my error say Level 14 when the catalog says severity 16?
answer: Both are real. The template sits in sys.messages at severity 16, and the engine raises it at Level 14 when a session hits it. Measured on SQL Server 2025 while writing this post.
post_title: Database in Recovery Pending: Cannot Be Opened (SQL Server Error 945)

question: I closed every window and it still fails.
answer: Object Explorer holds its own connection and reconnects on its own. Expanding the database node is enough to take one. Run the statement from a window whose context is master, and trust sys.dm_exec_sessions rather than the SSMS interface.
post_title: The Database Could Not Be Exclusively Locked to Perform the Operation (Error 5030)

question: I set SINGLE_USER and now I cannot get back in.
answer: An application pool has taken the one available connection. Find the holder in sys.dm_exec_sessions from master, KILL it, then run SET MULTI_USER immediately. If you keep losing the race, stop the application or take the database offline.
post_title: The Database Could Not Be Exclusively Locked to Perform the Operation (Error 5030)

question: Is WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE safe?
answer: It is decisive, not safe. It rolls back every open transaction in that database rather than waiting for them, so it belongs in a maintenance window. Other people’s in-flight work is what gets rolled back.
post_title: The Database Could Not Be Exclusively Locked to Perform the Operation (Error 5030)

question: Which statements raise 5030, and what do the states mean?
answer: Measured on SQL Server 2025 with one other session sitting in the database: ALTER DATABASE... MODIFY NAME raises 5030 with State 2 and ALTER DATABASE... COLLATE raises it with State 5, both immediately. SET SINGLE_USER does not raise it: without a termination clause it waits for the other session to leave, and WITH NO_WAIT fails with Msg 5070 instead. DROP DATABASE with a session inside fails with Msg 3702. Same cause every time, different message.
post_title: The Database Could Not Be Exclusively Locked to Perform the Operation (Error 5030)

question: Can I just set the database to EMERGENCY and then back to ONLINE?
answer: You can try it, and it costs nothing, because SET ONLINE simply runs recovery again. If the cause was transient, such as a file that was locked or a disk that was full at the moment of startup, it comes back. If the cause is a damaged page, you get the same 824, 3313 and 3414 in the log and the same state afterwards. In this reproduction it failed every time, which is itself the evidence that the problem is on disk rather than in the moment.
post_title: Database Marked SUSPECT (Error 926): EMERGENCY, CHECKDB, or the Backup

question: Can I stop this happening again?
answer: You cannot stop a disk going bad, so the goal is to find it early and to always have the restore available. Keep PAGE_VERIFY CHECKSUM on, run DBCC CHECKDB on a schedule so corruption is found by you rather than by recovery, watch msdb.dbo.suspect_pages, and test that your backup chain actually restores. The checks are in Get Suspect Pages and Integrity Checks.
post_title: Database Marked SUSPECT (Error 926): EMERGENCY, CHECKDB, or the Backup

question: Everyone says to run REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS. Why are you telling me not to?
answer: Not never, but not first. It is the right command when you have no usable backup, and it is a deliberate trade of correctness for availability. Two things to know before you run it: it frequently will not run at all on a crashed database, which is what happened here with Msg 7929, and when it does run it resolves corruption by deallocating pages, so rows disappear and you find out which ones afterwards. If a restore is available it wins on every measure.
post_title: Database Marked SUSPECT (Error 926): EMERGENCY, CHECKDB, or the Backup

question: How do I know how much data I will lose?
answer: With a restore you can state it exactly: everything written after the last backup you can apply. If the recovery model is FULL and the log file is readable, take the tail first and the answer is usually nothing, which is what the lab run showed. With repair the honest answer before you run it is that you do not know, and after you run it you only know by comparing against something else.
post_title: Database Marked SUSPECT (Error 926): EMERGENCY, CHECKDB, or the Backup

question: My database says RECOVERY_PENDING, not SUSPECT. Is this still my page?
answer: Probably not. RECOVERY_PENDING usually means SQL Server could not get at a file rather than that the data is damaged, and the fix is normally a path, a permission or free space. Start at Error 945. Two exceptions send you back here: an Enterprise or Developer instance that deferred a transaction, and any log that carries an 824 next to the recovery failure.
post_title: Database Marked SUSPECT (Error 926): EMERGENCY, CHECKDB, or the Backup

question: Should I detach the database and reattach it, or attach it without the log file?
answer: No. A detached SUSPECT database often refuses to attach, and at that point your only copy is a pair of files no instance will open. Attaching without the log, or rebuilding the log, is a last resort that throws away every uncommitted and unflushed transaction and produces a database of unknown consistency. Nothing on this page needs either, and the restore route needs the database left exactly where it is.
post_title: Database Marked SUSPECT (Error 926): EMERGENCY, CHECKDB, or the Backup

question: Can I catch 1205 in TRY/CATCH and retry?
answer: Yes. Unlike a compile-time error, 1205 is raised while the batch runs, so a CATCH block sees it and can re-run the whole transaction, which the victim has already had rolled back. Bound the retries and add a short delay, and treat the retry as a way of surviving the symptom, not as the fix: the access-order problem above is still there.
post_title: Reading and Fixing a SQL Server Deadlock

question: Can I stop my transaction being chosen as the victim?
answer: SET DEADLOCK_PRIORITY HIGH makes another session more likely to be chosen, but it does not stop deadlocks happening. It moves the pain rather than fixing it, and is worth using only for a genuinely more important process.
post_title: Reading and Fixing a SQL Server Deadlock

question: Is a deadlock the same as blocking?
answer: No, and confusing them wastes time. Blocking is one transaction waiting, and it resolves on its own when the other finishes. A deadlock is two transactions waiting on each other, which can never resolve, so SQL Server kills one. If you are seeing Msg 1222 instead, that is a lock timeout, which is blocking.
post_title: Reading and Fixing a SQL Server Deadlock

question: Where do I find the deadlock graph?
answer: The system_health extended events session captures deadlock graphs by default and is running on every modern instance. You do not need to set up a trace to catch the next one, the last several are usually already there.
post_title: Reading and Fixing a SQL Server Deadlock

question: Can I take differentials in SIMPLE recovery?
answer: Yes. SIMPLE blocks log backups, not differentials, and Microsoft's own SIMPLE model restore example uses one. What you lose is point in time recovery: your best possible recovery point becomes your last full or differential.
post_title: SQL Server Differential vs Log Backup: Which One Restores What, and How the Chain Breaks

question: Do I restore every differential, or just one?
answer: Just the most recent. A differential is cumulative, not incremental: each one contains everything changed since the base, not since the previous differential. Restore the full, then the latest differential, then the log backups taken after it.
post_title: SQL Server Differential vs Log Backup: Which One Restores What, and How the Chain Breaks

question: Does a full backup truncate the log?
answer: No, and this is a persistent myth. Under FULL or BULK_LOGGED, truncation follows a log backup, not a data backup. A full backup actually blocks truncation while it runs, which shows up as ACTIVE_BACKUP_OR_RESTORE in log_reuse_wait_desc. A full backup does include enough of the log to make the restored database consistent, which is probably where the confusion started.
post_title: SQL Server Differential vs Log Backup: Which One Restores What, and How the Chain Breaks

question: Is msdb history the same as having the backups?
answer: No, and treating it as such has ended careers. msdb history is deleted by sp_delete_backuphistory, does not exist on a different server, and Microsoft warns that physical_device_name cannot be relied on as a restore path. The history tells you what the chain looked like. Only the files let you use it.
post_title: SQL Server Differential vs Log Backup: Which One Restores What, and How the Chain Breaks

question: Why did my restore fail with a broken LSN chain?
answer: Usually one of 3 things. A log backup is missing from the sequence, someone recovered the database part way through with WITH RECOVERY instead of NORECOVERY, or the differential you are restoring belongs to a different full than the one you restored. The query above answers the third in seconds: match the differential's differential_base_lsn against the checkpoint_lsn of your fulls.
post_title: SQL Server Differential vs Log Backup: Which One Restores What, and How the Chain Breaks

question: Is IGNORE_DUP_KEY a fix?
answer: It converts the error into a warning by silently discarding the duplicate rows. In a controlled staging load that can be deliberate; on a production table it turns a loud, diagnosable failure into quiet data loss. Fix the source, not the signal.
post_title: Violation of PRIMARY KEY Constraint and Cannot Insert Duplicate Key (Errors 2627 and 2601)

question: The duplicate key value in the message is a row that is not in the table. I have checked.
answer: You are almost certainly looking at a value that compares equal but does not look equal. Two cases cover most of it. Trailing spaces are ignored in comparison, so inserting 'ABC' and then 'ABC ' into a unique index raises Msg 2601 and prints the duplicate key as (ABC ), which reads as a different row on screen. And on a case-insensitive collation, the default here, 'abc' and 'ABC' collide and the message prints (ABC). Search with WHERE LEN(col) <> DATALENGTH(col) for the padding case, and add COLLATE Latin1_General_BIN2 to your lookup to see case as SQL Server does not.
post_title: Violation of PRIMARY KEY Constraint and Cannot Insert Duplicate Key (Errors 2627 and 2601)

question: Which one will I get, 2627 or 2601?
answer: 2627 when a constraint blocks the row (primary key or unique constraint), 2601 when a unique index does. The investigation is identical either way, and the message names the object and the duplicate value in both cases.
post_title: Violation of PRIMARY KEY Constraint and Cannot Insert Duplicate Key (Errors 2627 and 2601)

question: Why did this only start failing in production?
answer: Volume and concurrency. Natural keys that never collided in dev collide at scale, and check-then-insert code that was safe single-user loses the race when two sessions insert the same key at once. The UPDLOCK/HOLDLOCK pattern in the post closes that gap.
post_title: Violation of PRIMARY KEY Constraint and Cannot Insert Duplicate Key (Errors 2627 and 2601)

question: Can I downgrade in place?
answer: No. There is no supported in-place downgrade path, which is why the runbook routes you into a side-by-side migration instead.
post_title: SQL Server Edition Change Runbook: Upgrade and Downgrade

question: Does an edition upgrade need an outage?
answer: It needs a restart, so plan for one. The setup itself is usually quick; the outage is the restart and the recovery of large databases afterwards.
post_title: SQL Server Edition Change Runbook: Upgrade and Downgrade

question: What most often blocks a Standard downgrade?
answer: Readable secondaries, then online index rebuilds hiding inside maintenance plans. TDE belongs on that list only if you are on SQL Server 2017 or earlier, because it moved to Standard in 2019. The last one is quiet: nothing fails until the next maintenance run.
post_title: SQL Server Edition Change Runbook: Upgrade and Downgrade

question: Will Enterprise features turn on automatically after upgrading?
answer: No. The upgrade removes the restriction, it does not configure anything. Compression, online rebuilds and the availability features all still need someone to enable them.
post_title: SQL Server Edition Change Runbook: Upgrade and Downgrade

question: Can I tell which server has the problem from the message?
answer: Partly, and better than most people realise. The 1418 is raised by the instance you ran the statement on, and the address in the message is the one it failed to reach, so the fault is at that address or on the path to it. If your own endpoint were the problem you would be looking at Msg 1486 instead, as check 1 shows. After that the error log line narrows it to one of four causes.
post_title: The Server Network Address Cannot Be Reached or Does Not Exist (Error 1418)

question: I opened port 5022 on the firewall and I still get 1418.
answer: Then 5022 was probably not the port. Nothing makes 5022 a default, it is only a convention, and the real number is whatever sys.tcp_endpoints reports, which the first check shows. The other two frequent cases are a rule added on only one of the two servers, and a rule on the wrong firewall profile. Confirm with Test-NetConnection from the complaining server before changing anything else.
post_title: The Server Network Address Cannot Be Reached or Does Not Exist (Error 1418)

question: Is 1418 an Availability Group error or a mirroring error?
answer: Both, because they share the object. Database mirroring is deprecated but an Availability Group replica still talks over a DATABASE_MIRRORING endpoint, which is why the AG wizard raises a mirroring error number and why sys.database_mirroring_endpoints is the right view to query on an AG node. Everything on this page applies to either.
post_title: The Server Network Address Cannot Be Reached or Does Not Exist (Error 1418)

question: The address works in SSMS, so why can mirroring not reach it?
answer: Because they are different ports and different listeners. SSMS connects to the database engine, normally 1433, while the partner address is the mirroring endpoint, normally 5022. A server can be perfectly reachable for queries and completely unreachable for mirroring. The lab proved the opposite case too: pointing the partner address at a live database engine port returned 1418 with error 4, An error occurred while receiving data in the log, because something answered and then spoke the wrong protocol.
post_title: The Server Network Address Cannot Be Reached or Does Not Exist (Error 1418)

question: What do I check first if I have no error log access?
answer: Work the checks in the order on this page, because they are ordered by how often each one is the answer and by how cheap each is to test: endpoint exists and is STARTED, port listening from the other server, CONNECT granted on the endpoint, name resolving to the right machine, firewall on both sides. You will find it, it just takes longer than reading one log line would have.
post_title: The Server Network Address Cannot Be Reached or Does Not Exist (Error 1418)

question: Can TRY...CATCH handle every error?
answer: No. TRY...CATCH does not catch severity 20 and above, compile errors in the same batch, or most connection-level failures. It is for statement-level problems, not for anything that kills the session.
post_title: SQL Server Error Severities Explained

question: The error number is not in any of these posts. What now?
answer: Look up the severity first, because that tells you whether it is a statement problem or a server problem, and the two need completely different responses. sys.messages holds every message text and severity the instance knows about.
post_title: SQL Server Error Severities Explained

question: Which severity levels should actually wake someone up?
answer: Severity 17 and above. Below that the statement failed but the server is fine, and it belongs in a morning report rather than a phone call. Severity 20 and above close the connection and get written to the error log, so those are the ones worth alerting on.
post_title: SQL Server Error Severities Explained

question: Why do some errors never reach my application?
answer: Severity 20 and above terminate the connection, so the client often sees a generic transport failure rather than the real message. The SQL Server error log has the truth, which is why almost every post in this series starts by reading it.
post_title: SQL Server Error Severities Explained

question: The error is not listed here.
answer: The pool grows as errors come up. In the meantime sys.messages holds every message text and severity the instance knows about, and the severity alone tells you whether you are dealing with a statement problem or a server problem. Error Severities Explained, first in Related Scripts below, is the page that turns that number into a decision.
post_title: SQL Server Errors: The Complete Guide

question: Where does SQL Server keep the real error?
answer: The SQL Server error log, which is not the same as what the client is shown. Read it with EXEC xp_readerrorlog 0, 1, N'search term'; or open ERRORLOG in the instance's Log folder if you cannot connect at all.
post_title: SQL Server Errors: The Complete Guide

question: Which errors should actually wake someone up?
answer: Severity 17 and above. Below that a statement failed and the server is fine. Severity 20 to 25 close the connection and get written to the error log, so those are the ones worth alerting on.
post_title: SQL Server Errors: The Complete Guide

question: Why did my application see a different error?
answer: Severity 20 and above terminate the connection, so the client often reports a generic transport failure instead of the real message. That is why the error log is the first stop rather than the last.
post_title: SQL Server Errors: The Complete Guide

question: Can I remove PRIMARY?
answer: No. PRIMARY holds the database metadata and cannot be removed or left empty. If your goal is to get user data off PRIMARY, that is done by moving objects elsewhere and changing the default filegroup, not by removing it.
post_title: The Filegroup Cannot Be Removed Because It Is Not Empty (Error 5042)

question: DBCC SHRINKFILE with EMPTYFILE is failing.
answer: Usually because there is nowhere for the pages to go. EMPTYFILE moves them to other files in the same filegroup, so it cannot work on the only file unless the file is already empty. It will also stop on objects it cannot move, which points you back at what is still on the filegroup.
post_title: The Filegroup Cannot Be Removed Because It Is Not Empty (Error 5042)

question: I dropped the table and it still will not remove.
answer: The files are still there. Dropping objects and removing files are two separate steps, and the filegroup counts as non-empty while it still owns a file. Run REMOVE FILE for each file, then remove the filegroup.
post_title: The Filegroup Cannot Be Removed Because It Is Not Empty (Error 5042)

question: Is there any risk of data loss?
answer: Not from the error itself, which is SQL Server refusing to do something destructive. The risk is in the steps you take to get around it. Rebuilding a clustered index moves real data, and EMPTYFILE relocates pages, so take a backup first and do it in a window.
post_title: The Filegroup Cannot Be Removed Because It Is Not Empty (Error 5042)

question: Why does the message say filegroup sometimes and file other times?
answer: Because 5042 is a shared message. In sys.messages the text is The %S_MSG '%.*ls' cannot be removed because it is not empty, and SQL Server fills in which kind of object it is talking about. The fix is the same idea either way: empty it first.
post_title: The Filegroup Cannot Be Removed Because It Is Not Empty (Error 5042)

question: Can this happen to an index rather than a table?
answer: Yes. The message lists indexes and LOB columns for that reason. An index built ON an empty filegroup hits the same wall as soon as it has rows to write, which for a populated table is at build time. On an empty table the CREATE INDEX succeeds too, measured on SQL Server 2025, so it is the same trap: nothing complains until data arrives.
post_title: The Filegroup Has No Files Assigned to It (Error 622)

question: Could I just put the table on PRIMARY instead?
answer: You could, and sometimes that is the right call if the filegroup was created by mistake. But if it was created deliberately, to keep user data off PRIMARY or to sit on different storage, moving the table to PRIMARY throws away the reason it existed. Add the file.
post_title: The Filegroup Has No Files Assigned to It (Error 622)

question: Do I have to drop and recreate the table?
answer: No. The table definition is fine and nothing about it is wrong. Add a file to the filegroup and the existing table starts working immediately, with its indexes and permissions intact.
post_title: The Filegroup Has No Files Assigned to It (Error 622)

question: Is this the same as the filegroup being full?
answer: No, and they are easy to confuse. 622 means there is no file at all. 1105 means there is a file and it has run out of room. Adding a file fixes both, but only 1105 also responds to autogrowth and disk space.
post_title: The Filegroup Has No Files Assigned to It (Error 622)

question: Why did CREATE TABLE not fail?
answer: Because creating a table is a metadata operation, and the filegroup exists as metadata. Nothing needs a page until a row is written, so that is where the check happens. Verified on SQL Server 2025: the create succeeded and only the insert raised 622.
post_title: The Filegroup Has No Files Assigned to It (Error 622)

question: ALTER INDEX REORGANIZE failed with 1105 but the database is nowhere near full.
answer: When an index spans several files in the filegroup and one of them is full, REORGANIZE stops when it tries to move rows into the full file. Microsoft's note on 1105 gives 2 ways out: rebuild the index instead, or raise the growth limit on the full file. The uneven-files case above is usually why one file filled first.
post_title: Could Not Allocate Space Because the Filegroup Is Full (Error 1105)

question: Autogrowth is on and the disk has room. Why did it still fail?
answer: Look at max_size in the query above. A file can have growth switched on and still stop dead at a MAXSIZE somebody set years ago, and even UNLIMITED is a 16 TB ceiling, which the message now says out loud. Reproduced on SQL Server 2025 with an 8 MB file capped at 8 MB: the insert fails at the cap however much disk is free.
post_title: Could Not Allocate Space Because the Filegroup Is Full (Error 1105)

question: Is this the same as the transaction log being full?
answer: No, and it is the most common confusion. 1105 is the data file, 9002 is the log. Taking a log backup does nothing for 1105.
post_title: Could Not Allocate Space Because the Filegroup Is Full (Error 1105)

question: Should I add a second data file?
answer: It is the right answer when the volume is genuinely full, because SQL Server spreads new allocations across files. But it is a permanent decision: the file has to be backed up, restored and managed forever after. If it is meant to be temporary, plan how it comes back out.
post_title: Could Not Allocate Space Because the Filegroup Is Full (Error 1105)

question: The disk has plenty of space, so why is the file full?
answer: Autogrowth is almost certainly switched off, or the file has hit a MAXSIZE cap. A file with growth = 0 will never grow no matter how much disk is free, and volume monitoring will never see it coming.
post_title: Could Not Allocate Space Because the Filegroup Is Full (Error 1105)

question: How do I know which config values are non-default?
answer: Compare value with value_in_use in sys.configurations, and treat every difference as a question rather than a fault. Somebody set it deliberately, and finding out why is part of taking the server on.
post_title: The First Hour on a SQL Server You Have Never Seen

question: Is there anything worth changing on day one?
answer: Rarely. The exception is something actively dangerous and reversible, such as a backup job that has been failing silently. Even then, fix the job rather than the schema.
post_title: The First Hour on a SQL Server You Have Never Seen

question: What if the server has been up for a year?
answer: Then the cumulative performance counters describe a year, not today, and you should either start a snapshot-and-delta collection or accept that the numbers are a profile rather than a diagnosis. Do not clear the counters on a server you have owned for an hour.
post_title: The First Hour on a SQL Server You Have Never Seen

question: Why does edition come before performance?
answer: Because it changes what you are allowed to recommend, which is why edition is question one. Suggesting a feature the instance is not licensed for wastes the credibility you need for the recommendations that matter, and edition is a two-second check.
post_title: The First Hour on a SQL Server You Have Never Seen

question: Can I just disable the constraint?
answer: You can, and it costs more than it saves. NOCHECK CONSTRAINT switches the check off entirely, so orphan rows go in unchecked, and when you switch it back on the constraint stays is_not_trusted unless you validate it, which means the optimiser stops using it for join elimination while you still pay to maintain it. Re-enable it with WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT, which validates the existing data and clears the flag.
post_title: The DELETE Statement Conflicted With a FOREIGN KEY Constraint (Error 547)

question: Should I add ON DELETE CASCADE?
answer: Only for a genuine ownership relationship. It is right for order lines under an order, and dangerous on a lookup table, where one delete can silently remove millions of rows.
post_title: The DELETE Statement Conflicted With a FOREIGN KEY Constraint (Error 547)

question: Which table is actually blocking me?
answer: The message names it, including the database, table and column. On a wide schema it names the first blocker only, so query sys.foreign_keys for every table referencing the parent before you start.
post_title: The DELETE Statement Conflicted With a FOREIGN KEY Constraint (Error 547)

question: Why is ALTER TABLE raising 547?
answer: Because it is validating. Adding a foreign key, or re-enabling one WITH CHECK, checks every existing child row against the parent, and the first orphan fails the statement with the same 547, worded as the ALTER TABLE statement conflicted with the FOREIGN KEY constraint. Find the orphans with the LEFT JOIN query above and fix or delete them; adding the constraint WITH NOCHECK makes the statement succeed but leaves it untrusted.
post_title: The DELETE Statement Conflicted With a FOREIGN KEY Constraint (Error 547)

question: CPU is high but nothing is running. What now?
answer: Check what else is on the box: backup agents, antivirus scanning data files, a second instance, SSRS or SSIS on the same server. Then check the OS side with the topology script, because Windows trimming SQL Server's working set shows up as I/O and CPU that no query explains.
post_title: SQL Server High CPU: What to Check First, in Order

question: How do I know whether it was always like this?
answer: Query Store, if it was on, has the history per query and shows the plan change. Without it, the wait stats since the last restart give a rough shape, and the cumulative counters reset when the service restarts, so check the start time before trusting them.
post_title: SQL Server High CPU: What to Check First, in Order

question: Should I lower MAXDOP to fix high CPU?
answer: Almost never as the first move. Lowering MAXDOP makes every parallel query slower to reduce the CPU one of them is burning, which is the wrong trade. Find the query first (Steps 2 and 3); MAXDOP and cost threshold get set from the published guidance afterwards, and usually the fix is raising cost threshold, not lowering MAXDOP.
post_title: SQL Server High CPU: What to Check First, in Order

question: Task Manager says sqlservr.exe is at 100 percent. Is that the same thing?
answer: It is the same symptom seen from outside. SQL Server will use every core it is allowed to when there is work, so the number on its own is not a fault; what matters is whether the work is legitimate. Step 1 answers that in one interval: a busy server with sensible waits is fine, a busy server running one runaway query is not.
post_title: SQL Server High CPU: What to Check First, in Order

question: Does error 102 appear in the SQL Server error log?
answer: No. sys.messages shows is_event_logged = 0 for 102, 156 and 105 alike. There is no server-side record to go back for, so whatever the application captured at the time is all the evidence there will be.
post_title: Incorrect Syntax Near in SQL Server (Error 102)

question: How do I know whether it is a real typo or a compatibility problem?
answer: Run the identical statement under SET PARSEONLY ON in a database at the current level, such as master. If it parses there and not in yours, the text is fine and the level is the difference. If it fails in both, it is a typo, and the quoted token tells you roughly where to look.
post_title: Incorrect Syntax Near in SQL Server (Error 102)

question: Is Msg 102 the same as Msg 156?
answer: No. 156 fires when the token is a reserved word, which is a narrower and more useful signal: either you used a keyword as a name, or a clause is in the wrong order. Both are severity 15. A trailing comma before FROM returns 156, not 102, which surprises people who have filed every syntax error under 102.
post_title: Incorrect Syntax Near in SQL Server (Error 102)

question: The query works on my dev server and fails in production. Same script, same version.
answer: Compare compatibility_level on the two databases, not the two instances. The engine version being identical is not enough, and a database restored from an older server keeps its old level indefinitely. This is the single most common cause of a 102 that "should not happen".
post_title: Incorrect Syntax Near in SQL Server (Error 102)

question: Why does the error point at something that is obviously correct?
answer: Because the quoted token is where the parser stopped, not where the statement went wrong. In the measured TRIM(LEADING '0' FROM '007') case it blamed '0', a perfectly valid literal, when the unrecognised keyword was LEADING just before it. Read leftwards from the token, not at it.
post_title: Incorrect Syntax Near in SQL Server (Error 102)

question: Will raising the compatibility level break anything?
answer: It can. The level drives optimizer behaviour as well as the grammar, so execution plans on unrelated statements can change. Raise it deliberately, with Query Store on so you can see what moved and revert a regressed plan, rather than as a quick fix for one parse error.
post_title: Incorrect Syntax Near in SQL Server (Error 102)

question: Could this be a permissions problem instead?
answer: Not directly. Referencing an object you have no rights on returns Msg 229, naming the object and the permission, and a cross-database reference with no user account in the target returns Msg 916. Both were measured rather than assumed. Permissions do reach you through the back door though: you cannot see an object you have no rights on, so OBJECT_ID() returns NULL and any tool that probes with it will tell you the object does not exist. Use HAS_PERMS_BY_NAME to tell "absent" apart from "not for you".
post_title: Invalid Object Name in SQL Server (Error 208)

question: It works for me but not for my colleague.
answer: Almost always the default schema. An unqualified name resolves against the caller’s schema first, so two people can run identical SQL and read different tables. Qualifying every object as schema.object removes the whole class of problem.
post_title: Invalid Object Name in SQL Server (Error 208)

question: It works in SSMS and fails in the application.
answer: Different database. Check DB_NAME() in both, then the connection string: the query is identical, the context is not.
post_title: Invalid Object Name in SQL Server (Error 208)

question: My editor underlines the table in red but the query runs fine.
answer: SSMS IntelliSense keeps a local cache of object names and does not notice objects created in another window or by another person. Press Ctrl + Shift + R to refresh it. The server was never involved.
post_title: Invalid Object Name in SQL Server (Error 208)

question: The procedure created without an error, so how can the table be missing?
answer: Deferred name resolution. SQL Server resolves object names when the statement runs, not when the procedure is created, so a clean deployment proves nothing about whether every referenced object exists.
post_title: Invalid Object Name in SQL Server (Error 208)

question: Why does my TRY/CATCH not catch 208?
answer: Because 208 happens at compile time, when the batch is bound, and a batch that will not compile never runs, including its CATCH. Move the reference into sp_executesql so binding happens at execution time, and the outer CATCH will see it.
post_title: Invalid Object Name in SQL Server (Error 208)

question: Can I just restore the single bad page?
answer: Page-level restore exists and is genuinely useful for a small number of pages, in full recovery model with an unbroken log chain. It is a real option once CHECKDB has told you the extent. It is not a way to skip finding out the extent, and it does not address why the page went bad.
post_title: Logical Consistency-Based I/O Error in SQL Server (Errors 823 and 824)

question: Does a clean DBCC CHECKDB mean the hardware is fine?
answer: It means the pages CHECKDB read were consistent at that moment. It says nothing about the drive that returned an error an hour ago. An 823 in particular is a storage-layer event that a later clean CHECKDB does not retract, so the hardware investigation runs regardless of the CHECKDB result.
post_title: Logical Consistency-Based I/O Error in SQL Server (Errors 823 and 824)

question: I got one 824 and everything seems fine now. Can I move on?
answer: No. The page is recorded in msdb.dbo.suspect_pages and the underlying cause has not changed. A single 824 with no other symptom is the best possible time to deal with this, because you still have a choice about when. Run CHECKDB, find the extent, and get the hardware looked at.
post_title: Logical Consistency-Based I/O Error in SQL Server (Errors 823 and 824)

question: Is 824 worse than 823?
answer: Neither is worse, they are different failures. 823 means the I/O request failed and the storage said so. 824 means the request succeeded and the data was wrong, which is more insidious because nothing below SQL Server flagged it. In practice 824 makes the storage team's job harder, because their monitoring will show a healthy path.
post_title: Logical Consistency-Based I/O Error in SQL Server (Errors 823 and 824)

question: What is error 605, and is it the same problem?
answer: Related but distinct. 605 is severity 21 and means a page was fetched that belongs to a different object than the allocation structures expect. That is allocation-level corruption rather than a failed read, and it goes straight to the restore conversation rather than the hardware one.
post_title: Logical Consistency-Based I/O Error in SQL Server (Errors 823 and 824)

question: Why did nothing alert me?
answer: Because SQL Server ships with no alerts at all, so severity 24 reaches the error log and the Windows event log and stops there. Checked on a real instance: zero alerts configured for 823, 824 or 825. Adding them is the single highest-value ten minutes available here.
post_title: Logical Consistency-Based I/O Error in SQL Server (Errors 823 and 824)

question: CPU is at 100 percent. Does that mean I need more cores?
answer: Usually not, and buying them is the expensive way to find out. A single bad plan scanning a table it should seek, running on every core, will saturate any server you give it. Find the queries first with Get Top CPU Queries, then decide. The ordered checklist for this branch is SQL Server High CPU.
post_title: SQL Server Is Slow: What to Check First, in Order

question: Everything is slow but no single query looks bad.
answer: That is the classic shape of blocking, or of a resource ceiling, and both are invisible if you only look at query duration. Check the blocker column first, because a chain of 200 short queries each waiting 3 seconds on one open transaction produces exactly this report. If nothing is blocked, run the interval wait query in Step 3: the answer to "everything is slow" is a wait type, not a query.
post_title: SQL Server Is Slow: What to Check First, in Order

question: How do I know if it is the server or the network?
answer: Compare elapsed time against CPU time for the request. A query that burned 9 seconds of CPU in 10 seconds of elapsed time was working, and the server owns it. A query that used 0.2 seconds of CPU in 40 seconds of elapsed time was waiting, and wait_type says what for. If that wait is ASYNC_NETWORK_IO the server had the rows ready and something downstream was not taking them. The cannot connect route is the ordered walkthrough for the other direction, when the client cannot reach the instance at all.
post_title: SQL Server Is Slow: What to Check First, in Order

question: It is slow only from the application. The same query is instant in SSMS.
answer: Three causes, and they are told apart quickly. First, the application and SSMS are not sending the same thing: a parameterised call from a driver can get a different plan from the literal you pasted in, which is the parameter sniffing case above. Second, SET options differ between the two connections, so they get separate cached plans and one of them is bad. Third, the engine finished quickly and the application is slow to consume the results, which shows as ASYNC_NETWORK_IO in the waits and is a client or network problem, not a database one.
post_title: SQL Server Is Slow: What to Check First, in Order

question: SQL Server is slow all of a sudden. Where do I start?
answer: Step 1, and only Step 1. Run the active requests query and read the blocker column. Sudden means something is happening now, so a snapshot of now answers it and a dashboard of the last 24 hours does not. If the blocker column has a value you are in a blocking incident, which is Step 2 and nothing else. If it does not, Step 3 tells you which resource to look at and you have skipped four wrong guesses.
post_title: SQL Server Is Slow: What to Check First, in Order

question: Should I just restart SQL Server?
answer: It will probably help for an hour and it destroys the evidence. A restart clears the plan cache, resets every wait statistic and rolls back the open transaction that was causing it, so the incident ends and nobody learns which of those four things fixed it. It also comes back. Capture the active requests and the interval waits first, which takes under a minute, then restart if you must.
post_title: SQL Server Is Slow: What to Check First, in Order

question: The query was fast yesterday and slow today, and nothing was deployed.
