answer: That is Step 7 and it is almost always a plan. The same text compiles to a different plan when statistics update, when the cache is cleared by a restart or a memory event, or when the first execution after a recompile happened to use an unusual parameter value. Get Query Store Regressions and Forced Plans names the query and the date the plan changed. If it is sensitive to the parameter rather than the date, Parameter Sniffing in SQL Server is the one to read.
post_title: SQL Server Is Slow: What to Check First, in Order

question: Can I just grant permissions to NT AUTHORITY\ANONYMOUS LOGON?
answer: No, and you should not try. It is not an account somebody forgot to add, it is the name for a connection with no identity attached. Granting it anything would mean granting it to every unauthenticated connection the instance ever receives. The fix is to make the hop carry an identity, by delegation or by an explicit login mapping.
post_title: Linked Server: Login Failed for User NT AUTHORITY\ANONYMOUS LOGON, and Error 7391 Distributed Transactions

question: I killed the linked server query and it has been in KILLED/ROLLBACK for 10 minutes. Do I restart SQL Server?
answer: Not yet. Check the wait type first. If it is still OLEDB or a PREEMPTIVE wait, the session is parked in a provider call and will end when that call does, so the question is what is holding the far end, not what is wrong locally. A restart rolls the transaction back during recovery instead, which is not faster, and it takes every other connection with it.
post_title: Linked Server: Login Failed for User NT AUTHORITY\ANONYMOUS LOGON, and Error 7391 Distributed Transactions

question: Is setting remote proc transaction promotion to false safe?
answer: It is safe when the remote work does not need to be atomic with the local work, and it is not safe when it does. With the option off, the remote call commits independently, so a later failure on the local side leaves the remote change in place with nothing to roll it back. It also only applies to remote stored procedure calls, so a four-part-name write inside a transaction still needs MS DTC either way.
post_title: Linked Server: Login Failed for User NT AUTHORITY\ANONYMOUS LOGON, and Error 7391 Distributed Transactions

question: The query works until I wrap it in BEGIN TRANSACTION. Why?
answer: Because that promotes it. A distributed query inside a local transaction is automatically escalated to a distributed transaction, so MS DTC joins in and now has to be running and reachable on both machines. Running the same statement with no explicit transaction open is the fastest confirmation that this is what you have, and it is the difference between an MS DTC problem and a security one.
post_title: Linked Server: Login Failed for User NT AUTHORITY\ANONYMOUS LOGON, and Error 7391 Distributed Transactions

question: Which is better, fixing delegation or mapping a fixed login?
answer: Delegation is better where the remote server's permissions are meant to differ per user, because it keeps each caller's own identity on the far side and keeps the remote audit trail honest. A fixed mapping is better where the linked server exists to serve one application or one report, because it is quick, it survives account changes, and it does not need anybody in Active Directory. What is not acceptable is a fixed mapping to a high-privilege login, since every caller inherits it.
post_title: Linked Server: Login Failed for User NT AUTHORITY\ANONYMOUS LOGON, and Error 7391 Distributed Transactions

question: Why does it work on the server and fail from my desktop?
answer: Because from the server there is one hop and from your desktop there are two. On the server you authenticated to that machine directly, so it holds a credential it can use to open the second connection as you. From your desktop it holds only an impersonation token, and NTLM impersonation cannot be forwarded. Nothing about your permissions differs between the two cases, which is why checking permissions wastes the first 20 minutes.
post_title: Linked Server: Login Failed for User NT AUTHORITY\ANONYMOUS LOGON, and Error 7391 Distributed Transactions

question: Is this a deadlock?
answer: No, and the difference matters. A deadlock is two transactions waiting on each other and can never resolve, so SQL Server kills one (Msg 1205). A lock timeout is one transaction waiting on another that is perfectly healthy. Yours simply gave up first.
post_title: Lock Request Time Out Period Exceeded (Error 1222)

question: Should I just raise the timeout?
answer: That converts a fast failure into a slow one and hides the blocking. A query that hangs forever is harder to diagnose than one that errors. Deal with what is holding the lock.
post_title: Lock Request Time Out Period Exceeded (Error 1222)

question: The timeout happened but nothing is blocking now. What was it?
answer: Almost certainly a session that was sleeping with an open transaction and has since closed or committed. The locks went with it, so there is nothing left to see. Have the blocked-request query above ready for the next one, or capture it continuously with the Get Open Transactions script below.
post_title: Lock Request Time Out Period Exceeded (Error 1222)

question: Why did I get a timeout at all, when SQL Server waits forever by default?
answer: Something set one. Check SELECT @@LOCK_TIMEOUT. SSMS sets it in some dialogs, which is why people meet this while clicking around Object Explorer, and ORMs often set it globally in connection setup.
post_title: Lock Request Time Out Period Exceeded (Error 1222)

question: Can I skip a log backup?
answer: No. A log backup contains exactly the records between two LSNs and the next file starts where it ended, so a missing one is a hole nothing else fills. You can recover to the end of the last file before the gap, or start again from a full or differential taken after it. Those are the only two outcomes.
post_title: The Log in This Backup Set Is Too Recent or Too Early to Apply (Errors 4305, 4326 and 3159)

question: Does a differential change the order?
answer: It shortens it. Restore the full, then the newest differential, then only the logs taken after that differential. The logs between the full and the differential are already inside the differential, and applying one of them after it raises 4326.
post_title: The Log in This Backup Set Is Too Recent or Too Early to Apply (Errors 4305, 4326 and 3159)

question: I only have the.trn files and no msdb history. How do I order them?
answer: RESTORE HEADERONLY against each file returns FirstLSN, LastLSN and DatabaseBackupLSN without restoring anything. Sort by FirstLSN and each file's LastLSN should equal the next file's FirstLSN. A gap between two files is the missing backup.
post_title: The Log in This Backup Set Is Too Recent or Too Early to Apply (Errors 4305, 4326 and 3159)

question: I restored the same log twice and it worked. Is the chain wrong?
answer: No. On SQL Server 2025 re-applying the file just applied is accepted silently, because its range still contains the database's current position. It does no harm and proves nothing either way. 4326 only fires when the whole file is behind the current position.
post_title: The Log in This Backup Set Is Too Recent or Too Early to Apply (Errors 4305, 4326 and 3159)

question: Is WITH REPLACE the fix for 3159?
answer: Only if you have decided you do not want the work since the last log backup. It overwrites the tail without any further warning, which in testing turned a five-row table into a four-row one. For anything you care about, BACKUP LOG... WITH NORECOVERY first, then restore, then apply that tail file last.
post_title: The Log in This Backup Set Is Too Recent or Too Early to Apply (Errors 4305, 4326 and 3159)

question: The tail-log backup fails because the data file is gone. Now what?
answer: Microsoft's documented route is BACKUP LOG... WITH NO_TRUNCATE for an offline database, and CONTINUE_AFTER_ERROR on a damaged one, which can succeed only if the log file itself is intact. If neither works, every transaction since the last log backup is lost and the honest restore ends at that file.
post_title: The Log in This Backup Set Is Too Recent or Too Early to Apply (Errors 4305, 4326 and 3159)

question: Which file do I restore next?
answer: The one whose LSN range contains the second number in the message. That number is where the database is right now. Run the msdb.dbo.backupset query in Read the Two LSNs and find the row where first_lsn is at or below it and last_lsn is above it. If no row qualifies, the file you need was never recorded here, or was deleted.
post_title: The Log in This Backup Set Is Too Recent or Too Early to Apply (Errors 4305, 4326 and 3159)

question: Can this bite me in SIMPLE recovery?
answer: Yes, and this is the most common misunderstanding on the topic. SIMPLE means you cannot take log backups, so LOG_BACKUP will never appear. It does not mean the log cannot fill. ACTIVE_TRANSACTION stops truncation under every recovery model, so one forgotten open transaction will grow a SIMPLE database's log until the disk does.
post_title: SQL Server Log Won’t Truncate: What log_reuse_wait_desc Is Telling You

question: I took a log backup and it still says LOG_BACKUP.
answer: If that log had never been backed up before, that is expected. Microsoft: “If the log has never been backed up, you must create two log backups to permit the Database Engine to truncate the log to the point of the last backup.” Take a second one. If it persists past that, re-run the query, because the reason has probably changed to something else.
post_title: SQL Server Log Won’t Truncate: What log_reuse_wait_desc Is Telling You

question: Is there an official query for this?
answer: Not a short one. The sys.databases reference page has three examples and none of them touch this column. What Microsoft does publish is a roughly 150 line diagnostic script, and it lives on the error 9002 troubleshooting page, not on the catalog view page. The three-column query above is the version you can actually remember at 2am.
post_title: SQL Server Log Won’t Truncate: What log_reuse_wait_desc Is Telling You

question: My log is still huge after I fixed the wait. Why?
answer: Because truncation and shrinking are different things. Truncation frees space inside the file for reuse. It never makes the file smaller on disk. Microsoft puts it plainly: “Shrinking a log file alone can't solve the problem of a full log file. Instead, you must discover why the log file is full and can't be truncated.” Fix the reason first, then decide whether the file is genuinely the wrong size.
post_title: SQL Server Log Won’t Truncate: What log_reuse_wait_desc Is Telling You

question: Why does my value not appear in Microsoft's list?
answer: Ids 10, 11 and 12 are documented only as “For internal use only” with no published description, and they are expected to be rare and short-lived. If you catch one, re-query rather than investigate. Anything else is worth reporting, because the documented set is small and stable.
post_title: SQL Server Log Won’t Truncate: What log_reuse_wait_desc Is Telling You

question: Does disabling the login disconnect it?
answer: No. Per Microsoft's ALTER LOGIN reference, disabling does not affect connections that already exist; it stops the next login. The account also keeps its permissions and can still be impersonated with EXECUTE AS. If the point is to stop someone now, find their sessions in sys.dm_exec_sessions and KILL them after the DISABLE.
post_title: Login Failed: The Account Is Disabled (Error 18470)

question: How do I find out who disabled it?
answer: Start with modify_date in sys.server_principals for when. The default trace holds recent ALTER LOGIN events, and a server audit, if configured, has the full answer.
post_title: Login Failed: The Account Is Disabled (Error 18470)

question: Should I enable it or recreate it?
answer: Enable it. Dropping and recreating a login generates a new SID for SQL logins, which orphans every database user mapped to it. Enabling changes nothing but the flag.
post_title: Login Failed: The Account Is Disabled (Error 18470)

question: Why does the client see the reason when a wrong password stays vague?
answer: A wrong password is deliberately vague so the message cannot be used to probe accounts. A disabled account is treated as safe to announce on current drivers, which makes this the one login failure you can diagnose from the client message alone.
post_title: Login Failed: The Account Is Disabled (Error 18470)

question: Lots of 18456s and I do not know which machine they are coming from.
answer: The error log records the caller on every one. Read it with EXEC xp_readerrorlog 0, 1, N'Login failed'; and each entry ends with the source, like [CLIENT: 10.0.0.25], alongside the login name and the reason. That turns "something is hammering us" into an address you can chase. Watch for a regular interval in the timestamps: a failure landing every fifteen minutes on the dot is a scheduled job or a monitoring agent, not a person mistyping a password, and the reason text usually names the database it could not open.
post_title: Troubleshoot “Login Failed for User” (Error 18456) in SQL Server

question: The password is definitely right, so why State 8?
answer: Check whether the login is locked out rather than wrong. A non-zero BadPasswordCount with a recent password change usually means an application is still retrying an old password, which is also what locks the account.
post_title: Troubleshoot “Login Failed for User” (Error 18456) in SQL Server

question: There is no 18456 in the error log at all. What now?
answer: Then the connection never reached authentication, and this is not a login problem. Look at the pre-login handshake instead, which fails earlier and reports a different error.
post_title: Troubleshoot “Login Failed for User” (Error 18456) in SQL Server

question: Why does the client only ever show State 1?
answer: Deliberately. Telling the client the real reason would hand an attacker a checklist of which part of the login was wrong. The true state is written to the SQL Server error log instead, which is why reading the log is the first step rather than the last.
post_title: Troubleshoot “Login Failed for User” (Error 18456) in SQL Server

question: Can I connect while it runs to see progress?
answer: Not in my testing, not even over the DAC. You do not need to: the log file on disk is the progress bar, and Get-Content -Tail 40 -Wait against it is the only monitor that worked throughout the window.
post_title: Login Failed: Server Is in Script Upgrade Mode (Error 18401), and How Long to Wait Before You Worry

question: How do I know it has actually finished?
answer: Two lines within a hundredth of a second of each other: "SQL Server is now ready for client connections" and "Recovery is complete". Then SELECT SERVERPROPERTY('ProductVersion') shows the new build. If the ready line appears without "Recovery is complete", keep watching.
post_title: Login Failed: Server Is in Script Upgrade Mode (Error 18401), and How Long to Wait Before You Worry

question: I already restarted it twice. Have I made it worse?
answer: You have made it longer, not worse, as long as the log shows the upgrade lines starting again after each restart. Stop restarting, watch the log, and let this run finish. If instead the log shows a 912 on each attempt, the restarts were never going to help and the failed-script section is where you are.
post_title: Login Failed: Server Is in Script Upgrade Mode (Error 18401), and How Long to Wait Before You Worry

question: It says only an administrator can connect. I am sysadmin, so why am I refused?
answer: Because the word does not mean sysadmin. In both reproductions for this post, sa, a second login in the sysadmin role and the dedicated administrator connection were all refused with 18401 for the entire window, 24 refusals on the DAC alone. The DAC connected in the seconds before the first upgrade script started and again the moment the last one finished, which is no use mid-window. Treat the instance as closed until the log says "Recovery is complete".
post_title: Login Failed: Server Is in Script Upgrade Mode (Error 18401), and How Long to Wait Before You Worry

question: The application saw 18401 for two minutes and now it is fine. Do I need to do anything?
answer: Confirm "Recovery is complete" is in the log and the build number is the one you installed, then no. That was the patch finishing. What is worth doing before the next window is telling the application owners the window includes this phase, and checking the log for "Could not open database" lines, because any database that was offline during the run was skipped and needs sp_vupgrade_replication run once it is back.
post_title: Login Failed: Server Is in Script Upgrade Mode (Error 18401), and How Long to Wait Before You Worry

question: Do Windows logins need any of this?
answer: Less of it, and not none of it. A Windows login has no password or hash to carry, and its SID comes from Active Directory rather than from SQL Server, so the orphaned-user problem mostly disappears. The disabled flag, the default database, the default language and server role membership all still apply exactly as they do for SQL logins. The failure specific to Windows logins is a domain or trust boundary. Script it perfectly onto a server in a domain with no trust to the account's domain and it still cannot authenticate.
post_title: SQL Server Login Migration: What Gets Silently Left Behind

question: How do I know whether a password was carried across or re-typed?
answer: Compare the stored hash, not the password. The hash is salted, so creating two logins with the identical password produces two completely different hashes. That sounds unhelpful and is actually the useful property: if the hashes match between source and target, the login was genuinely scripted with WITH PASSWORD = <hash> HASHED. If they differ, somebody typed a password in by hand, and you now need to know whether they typed the right one.
post_title: SQL Server Login Migration: What Gets Silently Left Behind

question: Is sp_help_revlogin still the right tool in 2026?
answer: For what it does, yes, and it covers more than most people assume. Reading the source, it scripts the password hash, the SID, the default database, both password policy options, an ALTER LOGIN... DISABLE for disabled logins and a DENY CONNECT SQL where one exists. It is not deprecated and it still works. What it genuinely does not carry is DEFAULT_LANGUAGE and server role membership, and it has never claimed to handle credentials, proxies or contained users. The real risk is not the procedure. It is that people say "we scripted the logins" while having used something else entirely, such as SSMS Script Login as CREATE To, which emits neither the password nor the SID.
post_title: SQL Server Login Migration: What Gets Silently Left Behind

question: Is there a single query that tells me if the migration is complete?
answer: No, and be wary of anything that claims to be one. What you can have is a comparison: capture the same fingerprint from both servers and diff it. That turns “is it complete”, which nobody can answer from one server, into “what is different”, which is a question a text diff answers exactly.
post_title: SQL Server Login Migration: What Gets Silently Left Behind

question: Should I just use dbatools Copy-DbaLogin instead?
answer: If PowerShell against both servers is an option, it is the strongest tool for the job, and it is what most of the community now recommends: Copy-DbaLogin preserves the password hash and SID the same way, and unlike sp_help_revlogin it can carry server role memberships and server-level permissions across with it. It does not change the thesis of this post. Whichever tool produces your script, the question is still what it emits and what it silently skips. Credentials, linked server passwords and contained users sit outside every login transfer, and the checklist above is how you verify the target regardless of which tool built it.
post_title: SQL Server Login Migration: What Gets Silently Left Behind

question: What about logins that own databases or Agent jobs?
answer: Ownership is stored by SID as well, so it follows the same rule. A database whose owner SID no longer resolves shows a blank or unresolved owner, and Agent jobs owned by a missing login can fail to start. Re-point them deliberately with ALTER AUTHORIZATION ON DATABASE::[name] TO [login] rather than leaving them, and check job ownership as part of the same pass.
post_title: SQL Server Login Migration: What Gets Silently Left Behind

question: Why does my migrated login work but my database user has no permissions?
answer: Almost always a SID mismatch. A database user is bound to a login by SID, not by name. Recreate the login by name and it gets a fresh SID, so the user inside the restored database still points at the old one and is now orphaned. The login authenticates fine, which is what makes it confusing, and then has no rights inside the database. Confirm by comparing sys.server_principals.sid on the server with sys.database_principals.sid in the database. Fix with ALTER USER [name] WITH LOGIN = [name], which re-binds the user to the current login.
post_title: SQL Server Login Migration: What Gets Silently Left Behind

question: Can I just switch to SQL authentication?
answer: It makes the error go away because it stops using Windows identities entirely. That is sometimes the right call for a machine that cannot be domain-joined, but state it honestly as a decision, not a fix.
post_title: Login Failed: The Login Is From an Untrusted Domain (Error 18452)

question: Do I need the domain admins?
answer: Usually not first. One failing client is nearly always that client: a local account, an IP connection string, or a stale token. Many clients failing at the same moment is when the domain conversation earns its place.
post_title: Login Failed: The Login Is From an Untrusted Domain (Error 18452)

question: I am using SQL Server authentication and still got 18452.
answer: Then the Windows-trust reading is a red herring. Microsoft's page lists 2 non-Windows causes: the instance only accepts Windows authentication, or the SQL login you typed does not exist on it. Run SELECT SERVERPROPERTY('IsIntegratedSecurityOnly'); 1 means mixed mode is off and no SQL login gets in until it is switched on and the instance restarted. If it returns 0, check the login exists in sys.sql_logins.
post_title: Login Failed: The Login Is From an Untrusted Domain (Error 18452)

question: Why does connecting by IP matter?
answer: Kerberos identifies services by name, so an IP connection cannot use it and falls back to NTLM. Where policy restricts NTLM, that fallback surfaces as this error instead of working quietly.
post_title: Login Failed: The Login Is From an Untrusted Domain (Error 18452)

question: Can I install or remove SSMS across several machines without clicking through each one?
answer: Yes, see the scripted Install & Update and Uninstall links above. Both are silent by default, log what they did, and are built for fleet or repeat jump-host setups rather than a single interactive install.
post_title: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS): The Complete Guide

question: Can I run SSMS on Linux or macOS?
answer: No, SSMS itself is Windows-only. From Linux or macOS the supported option is now Visual Studio Code with the MSSQL extension, since Azure Data Studio was retired in February 2026, or a plain sqlcmd session for anything scriptable.
post_title: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS): The Complete Guide

question: Can I use git without leaving SSMS?
answer: Yes, since SSMS 21. The Git menu covers clone, branch, commit, push and stash against GitHub or Azure DevOps, which is enough to keep your scripts folder under version control on the jump host you already work from. It versions files, not the database; schema-as-source is what the separate Database DevOps workload (preview) is for.
post_title: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS): The Complete Guide

question: Does SSMS have a dark theme?
answer: Yes, officially, at last. SSMS 21 shipped the first supported dark theme and SSMS 22 extended theming further, adding new themes (and retiring the old Blue one) and bringing more of the dialogs into line. Pick a theme under Tools > Options and expect the odd unthemed dialog at the edges, the coverage has improved with each 22.x release.
post_title: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS): The Complete Guide

question: Is SSMS still being actively updated?
answer: Yes, more actively than it has been in years. It ships as a separate download from the SQL Server engine with its own release cadence, and the SSMS 22 line has been updating roughly monthly. See Install & Update above for where to get it and how the update checks work, and What Changed in SSMS 21 and 22 for the features worth knowing about.
post_title: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS): The Complete Guide

question: What do I need to use Copilot in SSMS, and does it cost anything?
answer: SSMS 22 or later, the AI Assistance workload ticked in the Visual Studio Installer, and a GitHub account. A free Copilot tier exists, so trying it costs nothing. It is opt-in per machine, code completions ship disabled by default, and as of 22.9 Ask mode cannot execute arbitrary queries against the connected server, which is the right default for anything production-shaped.
post_title: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS): The Complete Guide

question: What replaced Azure Data Studio?
answer: Visual Studio Code with the MSSQL extension. Azure Data Studio was retired on 28 February 2026 and no longer gets updates or security fixes, and Microsoft’s guidance is to move to VS Code, where existing queries, scripts and database projects open without conversion. For production DBA work it still isn’t an SSMS replacement: the object-level dialogs, SQL Server Agent management and the Maintenance Plan designer are only in SSMS.
post_title: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS): The Complete Guide

question: Why does SSMS suddenly refuse to connect after an update?
answer: Almost always the certificate chain trust error, current SSMS versions default to encrypting the connection and validating the server’s certificate, which older instances running a self-signed cert weren’t set up to satisfy. See Fix the Certificate Chain Trust Error above for the actual cause and fix.
post_title: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS): The Complete Guide

question: Does MAXDOP affect anything other than queries?
answer: Yes, and it catches people during maintenance windows. It also governs the parallelism of DBCC CHECKDB, CHECKTABLE and CHECKFILEGROUP, and index operations, though an index statement can override it with its own MAXDOP option.
post_title: SQL Server MAXDOP and Cost Threshold: What To Set, and Why 5 Is Not a Recommendation

question: Does SQL Server 2019 set MAXDOP for me?
answer: At install, yes. Setup detects the processor layout and writes a recommended value, and it does so even if you skip that page in the wizard. It is not ongoing self-configuration though, and the engine default for the setting is still 0. An in-place upgrade, a restored configuration or a manual reset all land you back on 0, so read the instance rather than assuming the version fixed it.
post_title: SQL Server MAXDOP and Cost Threshold: What To Set, and Why 5 Is Not a Recommendation

question: High CXPACKET means lower MAXDOP, right?
answer: Not any more, and this is the most out of date advice in circulation. CXPACKET has been narrowed twice. From SQL Server 2016 SP2 and 2017 CU3, consumer-side waiting split out into CXCONSUMER, which Microsoft calls “a normal part of parallel query execution”. From 2022, synchronisation split out again into CXSYNC_PORT and CXSYNC_CONSUMER. On a modern build CXPACKET means something much more specific than it did on 2014, so a big number is no longer evidence on its own.
post_title: SQL Server MAXDOP and Cost Threshold: What To Set, and Why 5 Is Not a Recommendation

question: What should I set cost threshold to?
answer: Microsoft does not say, and that is worth knowing before you accept a number from anyone. What they do say is that “the default value of 5 is a starting point, not a recommendation”, that raising it helps keep small OLTP queries serial, and that you should “use small increments and observe a full business cycle before further changes”. The widely repeated 50 is community consensus. It is a reasonable place to start, but cite it honestly.
post_title: SQL Server MAXDOP and Cost Threshold: What To Set, and Why 5 Is Not a Recommendation

question: Which setting wins if I set it in several places?
answer: Resource Governor is a ceiling nothing can exceed. Below that, a query hint beats the database scoped configuration, which beats sp_configure. Worth knowing that the query hints page opens by saying the hint “also overrides the Resource Governor” and only then explains that it is capped by it, which reads as the opposite of what it means.
post_title: SQL Server MAXDOP and Cost Threshold: What To Set, and Why 5 Is Not a Recommendation

question: How do I find the query that caused it after the fact?
answer: Query Store, if the database has it enabled, because it keeps memory grant figures per query with timestamps. Without it the live DMVs are gone the moment the grant is released, and the error log gives you the time of the 8645 but not the query that was holding the memory.
post_title: Insufficient System Memory and Memory Grant Timeouts (Errors 701 and 8645)

question: Is error 8623 the same problem?
answer: No. 8623 is severity 16 and means the query processor could not produce a plan because the statement was too complex, typically a generated query or a very large IN list. It is a compilation limit, not memory pressure, and it is fixed in the application rather than on the server.
post_title: Insufficient System Memory and Memory Grant Timeouts (Errors 701 and 8645)

question: My RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE waits look enormous. Is that the cause?
answer: Check the total against instance uptime before concluding anything. Measured while writing this post: 216 waits totalling over 18 hours on an instance up for 24 hours, with a single wait recorded at 8 hours. Both numbers were artifacts of parallel accumulation and a host that had been suspended. Take a delta over a window you choose, or read the live DMVs instead.
post_title: Insufficient System Memory and Memory Grant Timeouts (Errors 701 and 8645)

question: What is a normal reading for sys.dm_exec_query_memory_grants?
answer: Empty. On an instance with nothing queued it returns no rows, and waiter_count on the semaphore is 0. That is worth confirming on your own servers while they are healthy, so that rows appearing during an incident are immediately meaningful rather than something you have to interpret from scratch.
post_title: Insufficient System Memory and Memory Grant Timeouts (Errors 701 and 8645)

question: Which is worse, 701 or 8645?
answer: 701 is severity 19 and 8645 is severity 17, and that ordering reflects it. 701 means an allocation could not be satisfied, which is an instance-wide condition. 8645 is a timeout on a queue, and SQL Server's own message text tells you to rerun the query. Repeated 8645s still matter, they are just a different investigation.
post_title: Insufficient System Memory and Memory Grant Timeouts (Errors 701 and 8645)

question: Will more RAM fix error 8645?
answer: Usually not on its own. 8645 means the memory was already committed to other queries, so the question is which query took it and whether it deserved it. Adding RAM without raising max server memory changes nothing at all, and adding both still leaves an oversized grant taking an oversized share.
post_title: Insufficient System Memory and Memory Grant Timeouts (Errors 701 and 8645)

question: Can I add replicas running a newer SQL Server version?
answer: For a rolling upgrade the direction matters: you upgrade secondaries first, then fail over. What you cannot do is leave a mixed-version AG running as a permanent state.
post_title: SQL Server Migration Runbook: Availability Groups and Failover Clusters

question: Do I have to update DNS?
answer: Only if the listener name is changing. If it is, do it after validation and remember the TTL, because clients will keep the old record for as long as you told them to.
post_title: SQL Server Migration Runbook: Availability Groups and Failover Clusters

question: How do I know synchronisation is really finished?
answer: Look at the redo queue on the secondary rather than at a green health icon. Data that has arrived but not been applied is exactly the data that extends your failover time.
post_title: SQL Server Migration Runbook: Availability Groups and Failover Clusters

question: Which is less risky, AG or FCI migration?
answer: An AG migration, because the cutover is a planned failover you can reverse by failing back. An FCI cutover is a commitment, which is why its rollback procedure is a separate document rather than a paragraph.
post_title: SQL Server Migration Runbook: Availability Groups and Failover Clusters

question: Can I use this for a version upgrade at the same time?
answer: Yes, and that is the recommended way to upgrade. Restore onto a newer version on new hardware, which gives you a rollback that consists of pointing back at the old server.
post_title: SQL Server Migration Runbook: Standalone Instance

question: Do I need to match sp_configure exactly?
answer: Match it deliberately rather than exactly. Copy the settings that reflect decisions someone made, and take the opportunity to fix the ones that were only ever defaults, like MAXDOP or max server memory on a server that has since grown.
post_title: SQL Server Migration Runbook: Standalone Instance

question: How long before the window should Phase 0 run?
answer: Days, not hours. The whole point of a pre-migration assessment is that you can still act on what it finds. Running it the morning of the window turns findings into problems.
post_title: SQL Server Migration Runbook: Standalone Instance

question: What is most often forgotten?
answer: Agent jobs and linked servers, then database mail and credentials. The data moves because moving it is the obvious task; the surroundings move because someone made a list. Add certificates to that list: if anything is TDE-protected or backup-encrypted, the certificate has to be restored on the target before the database restore will even start.
post_title: SQL Server Migration Runbook: Standalone Instance

question: How do I check a column exists before I reference it?
answer: COL_LENGTH('schema.object', 'column') returns NULL when the column is not there, and it works for DMVs as well as tables. For a one-off look, query sys.all_columns for the object as in the first query on this page, or run the batch under SET NOEXEC ON, which binds every column name without executing anything.
post_title: Fix “Msg 207: Invalid Column Name” in SQL Server

question: I wrapped the column in an IF version check and it still fails. Why?
answer: Because the whole batch is bound at compile time, before the IF is evaluated, so a missing column fails the batch even inside a branch that never runs. Test with COL_LENGTH() and keep the guarded query in sp_executesql so it is only bound when it can succeed. Pattern 5 above shows both halves.
post_title: Fix “Msg 207: Invalid Column Name” in SQL Server

question: The column is definitely there. I can see it.
answer: Check the alias. If the query aliases a table and then references the column through a different alias, or through a derived table that does not project the column, SQL Server reports it as invalid even though the column exists.
post_title: Fix “Msg 207: Invalid Column Name” in SQL Server

question: The query works on one server and not another.
answer: Compare the two schemas rather than the query. A column added in one environment and never deployed to the other is the usual answer, and Get Schema Change History will date the change.
post_title: Fix “Msg 207: Invalid Column Name” in SQL Server

question: Is "error 40" a different error?
answer: Same failure, different label: error 40 is the Named Pipes provider reporting that it could not open a connection, and the bracketed OS error, 53 here, is the part that says why.
post_title: Could Not Open a Connection to SQL Server: Error 53 and Named Pipes Error 40

question: It works on the server itself but fails from everywhere else.
answer: That is the signature of TCP/IP disabled in Configuration Manager or a firewall blocking 1433. Local connections ride shared memory, which needs neither.
post_title: Could Not Open a Connection to SQL Server: Error 53 and Named Pipes Error 40

question: The default instance connects but the named instance does not.
answer: Named instances without a fixed port are discovered through the Browser service on UDP 1434. Block that and the named instance is invisible while the default instance works, which looks baffling until you know the mechanism.
post_title: Could Not Open a Connection to SQL Server: Error 53 and Named Pipes Error 40

question: The port is open. I tested it. So why am I still getting 53?
answer: Because 53 happens before the port. It is a Windows network error meaning the path could not be found, so the client never got as far as a SQL Server conversation. If Test-NetConnection <server> -Port 1433 succeeds but the name fails, you have proved the route and the port are fine and the name is the problem: connect by IP address, and if that works it is DNS, a stale HOSTS entry, or an alias in SQL Server Configuration Manager pointing somewhere that no longer exists. If the port test fails too, you are looking at a firewall or the wrong port, and the error you eventually get will not be 53.
post_title: Could Not Open a Connection to SQL Server: Error 53 and Named Pipes Error 40

question: Can I just enable the guest user?
answer: It makes the error go away by giving every login access to the database, which is why it shows up in security audits. Map a real user for the login instead; guest is the workaround that becomes a finding.
post_title: The Server Principal Is Not Able to Access the Database (Error 916)

question: Is this the same as login failed (18456)?
answer: No. 18456 means the server door did not open, authentication itself failed. 916 fires after a successful login: the server let the principal in and one specific database refused it. Password resets cannot fix it.
post_title: The Server Principal Is Not Able to Access the Database (Error 916)

question: The error came from an application with ODBC state 08004, not from SSMS.
answer: Then the code changed database after connecting: a USE, a three-part name such as OtherDb.dbo.Table, or a procedure that reaches into another database. That is the shape reproduced above. A database named in the connection string itself fails earlier and differently, with 4060, so 916 from an application points at a statement, not at the connection string.
post_title: The Server Principal Is Not Able to Access the Database (Error 916)

question: Why does SSMS raise this for a database I never clicked?
answer: Object Explorer queries every database for the detail columns it displays, size and collation included. If your login lacks access to any one database, that background query fails and SSMS surfaces 916 about a database you never touched. Remove those columns from Object Explorer Details or grant the access.
post_title: The Server Principal Is Not Able to Access the Database (Error 916)

question: I fixed the user and the application still cannot log in.
answer: Check the other databases. A restore from another server usually brings several databases across, and each one carries its own copy of the orphan, so fixing one database fixes one database. Run the orphan query in each, or use the Get Orphaned Users script below to see every database in one pass.
post_title: User, Group or Role Already Exists in the Current Database (Error 15023)

question: Should I just drop the user and recreate it?
answer: No. Dropping destroys the role memberships and object permissions the user already had, and the recreated one is empty. ALTER USER... WITH LOGIN remaps it and keeps everything.
post_title: User, Group or Role Already Exists in the Current Database (Error 15023)

question: What about sp_change_users_login Auto_Fix?
answer: Deprecated, and it matches by name, which is the guess that causes trouble when two different accounts share a name across servers. ALTER USER... WITH LOGIN is explicit and supported.
post_title: User, Group or Role Already Exists in the Current Database (Error 15023)

question: Why do Windows logins usually survive a restore?
answer: Their SID comes from Active Directory and is the same on every server. A SQL login SID is generated on the instance that created it, so it does not match anywhere else.
post_title: User, Group or Role Already Exists in the Current Database (Error 15023)

question: Is TrustServerCertificate=True the same as turning encryption off?
answer: No, and the difference matters. TrustServerCertificate=True keeps the channel encrypted and skips validating the certificate, so it connects you while an expired or untrusted certificate is still sitting there. Encrypt=False asks for no encryption at all and will not help you if the server has Force Encryption on, because the server still requires it. Use the first to confirm the certificate is the cause, then go and fix the certificate.
post_title: A Connection Was Successfully Established, But Then an Error Occurred During Login

question: SSMS connects fine from the same machine but the application fails.
answer: Different client stacks. SSMS carries its own driver and the application uses whatever it was built against, and Microsoft.Data.SqlClient changed its default to Encrypt=true at version 4.0, listed by MS Docs under breaking changes. An application that picked up a newer driver starts demanding encryption against a server whose certificate it will not accept, while SSMS on the same box carries on. Check the driver version and the connection string’s Encrypt setting before you touch the server.
post_title: A Connection Was Successfully Established, But Then an Error Occurred During Login

question: Should I check the firewall or the port?
answer: No, this error rules both out. The message says the connection was established, so the port was reachable and something was listening. A blocked or wrong port gives you a connect failure or a timeout with a different message entirely. What is left is everything that happens after the socket opens: protocol, encryption, certificate, or a device on the path sending a reset.
post_title: A Connection Was Successfully Established, But Then an Error Occurred During Login

question: The connections query returns rows and they all look fine.
answer: sys.dm_exec_connections can only show connections that got through, so it tells you nothing about the client that cannot. Use it to establish what a working client negotiates, then compare that against the failing client’s driver and connection string. The failed attempt leaves no row anywhere, which is the same reason there is no 18456 in the error log.
post_title: A Connection Was Successfully Established, But Then an Error Occurred During Login

question: I reassigned the schema and it still will not drop.
answer: Something else is owned. A role owned by the principal raises 15421 instead, which sends people looking for a different problem, and individual objects can carry an owner too. Check schemas, roles and objects in one query before you start.
post_title: The Database Principal Owns a Schema in the Database and Cannot Be Dropped (Error 15138)

question: Should I drop the schema or reassign it?
answer: Count the objects first. Empty and unreferenced, drop it. Holding anything at all, reassign it to dbo: that changes nothing about permissions and is the safer default when you are unsure.
post_title: The Database Principal Owns a Schema in the Database and Cannot Be Dropped (Error 15138)

question: Where does SSMS show which schema the user owns?
answer: Open the user under Security, Users, Properties, and the Owned Schemas page has it ticked. The tick is read-only there, because a schema must always have an owner: ownership moves from the schema side, in the schema's own Properties dialog or with ALTER AUTHORIZATION. The first query on this page shows the same thing for schemas, roles and objects in one result.
post_title: The Database Principal Owns a Schema in the Database and Cannot Be Dropped (Error 15138)

question: Why does the user own a schema I never created?
answer: When a user is created without an explicit DEFAULT_SCHEMA, some tooling creates a schema of the same name and makes the user its owner. After a migration you often find a row of empty, user-named schemas that exist for no other reason.
post_title: The Database Principal Owns a Schema in the Database and Cannot Be Dropped (Error 15138)

question: 825 keeps appearing in the error log. Is the disk failing?
answer: Treat a repeat as yes. One 825 is worth investigating, a pattern is a failing device, and the interval between occurrences shortening is the thing to watch. Run the xp_readerrorlog loop above across the older logs to date the first one, then take the offsets and timestamps to whoever owns the storage.
post_title: A Read of the File Succeeded After Failing (Error 825, the Read-Retry Warning)

question: It says it succeeded, so is there a problem?
answer: Yes. The data is fine right now and the hardware is not. SQL Server had to retry a read because the storage returned bad data. This is the warning that arrives before 823 and 824, which are the ones that take a database offline.
post_title: A Read of the File Succeeded After Failing (Error 825, the Read-Retry Warning)

question: Should I run REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS?
answer: No. Nothing is broken yet. That command is for confirmed corruption you cannot restore around, and it does exactly what its name says. Check your backups restore, run DBCC CHECKDB WITH PHYSICAL_ONLY, and take it to whoever owns the storage.
post_title: A Read of the File Succeeded After Failing (Error 825, the Read-Retry Warning)

question: Why did nothing alert me?
answer: Severity 10 is informational, so no default alert fires, no job fails and the application sees nothing. Setting an Agent alert on message 825 is the single most valuable thing in this post.
post_title: A Read of the File Succeeded After Failing (Error 825, the Read-Retry Warning)

question: Can I copy the mdf and ldf and attach them instead?
answer: No. That fails with error 948, severity 20, and the message says "a downgrade path is not supported" in those words. The version stamp lives in the data file itself, so the backup and the data file carry the same number.
post_title: Restore From a Newer SQL Server Version (Error 3169)

question: Can I restore a SQL Server 2022 backup to SQL Server 2019?
answer: No, and the same answer applies to every pair where the backup is the newer one. Restoring forward is supported and normal, restoring backward is not supported at all. The error you get is 3169 and it names both internal version numbers.
post_title: Restore From a Newer SQL Server Version (Error 3169)

question: How big a job is the script and copy route really?
answer: It scales with the data, not the schema. Generate Scripts with data included is fine for a small database and becomes unusable somewhere in the low gigabytes. Past that, script the schema without indexes, bcp the tables, then create the indexes and constraints, and expect the index build to be the longest step. Plan it as a migration with a tested rollback, not as a long restore.
post_title: Restore From a Newer SQL Server Version (Error 3169)

question: Is there a tool that downgrades a database?
answer: Not from Microsoft, and the third-party ones you will find are doing a schema and data export under a different name. If that is the route you are taking, use Generate Scripts, a dacpac, or bcp, where the behaviour is documented and the failures are visible.
post_title: Restore From a Newer SQL Server Version (Error 3169)

question: RESTORE HEADERONLY worked, so why will the restore not?
answer: The backup header is readable by older versions on purpose, which is how a restore tool can tell you what is in a file before trying it. The pages inside are in the newer format. HEADERONLY and FILELISTONLY both returned full results on the older instance while VERIFYONLY and RESTORE DATABASE both failed with 3169.
post_title: Restore From a Newer SQL Server Version (Error 3169)

question: What if I set the compatibility level down before taking the backup?
answer: It makes no difference. Compatibility level is a query behaviour setting, the internal database version is the physical file format, and only the second one is checked at restore time. A database at compatibility level 160 on a 2025 instance still has internal version 998 and still fails with 3169.
post_title: Restore From a Newer SQL Server Version (Error 3169)

question: Can I check a backup without restoring it?
answer: Yes, and you should. RESTORE VERIFYONLY reads and checks the whole backup, RESTORE HEADERONLY tells you what is in it, and RESTORE FILELISTONLY gives the logical file names for WITH MOVE. All three are read-only and none need the target database to exist.
post_title: RESTORE Is Terminating Abnormally (Errors 3013 and 3241)

question: Does 3241 always mean the backup is corrupt?
answer: Not necessarily. It means SQL Server cannot read the file as a backup, which also covers the wrong file entirely, a copy that never finished, a third-party format, and a backup from a newer version of SQL Server being restored to an older one. That last case is a common surprise and there is nothing wrong with the file.
post_title: RESTORE Is Terminating Abnormally (Errors 3013 and 3241)

question: How do I fix error 3013?
answer: You do not, directly. 3013 reports that the restore stopped, and it is the same message whatever went wrong. Find the error printed immediately before it: across five reproduced failures that was 3241, 3287, 3634 with 3156, 3102 or 3154, each with a completely different fix.
post_title: RESTORE Is Terminating Abnormally (Errors 3013 and 3241)

question: My tool only shows 3013. Now what?
answer: Rerun the restore by hand in SSMS or sqlcmd and read the whole output, or open the SQL Server error log, which records the real error even when the client showed only the closing line. Agent job history in particular truncates the useful part.
post_title: RESTORE Is Terminating Abnormally (Errors 3013 and 3241)

question: What is the difference between 3241 and 3287?
answer: 3241 is "this is not a backup media family I can process". 3287 is "this is a backup, and the file ID inside it cannot be read", which in testing came from a backup that had been truncated. 3287 points more strongly at an interrupted copy, so compare the file size against the source first.
post_title: RESTORE Is Terminating Abnormally (Errors 3013 and 3241)

question: Why did I get four errors before the 3013?
answer: Because a restore validates every file. In the reproduced bad-path case, each of the data file and the log file produced a 3634 and a 3156, then a line reading "Problems were identified while planning for the RESTORE statement. Previous messages provide details", then 3013. SQL Server is explicitly pointing you upwards.
post_title: RESTORE Is Terminating Abnormally (Errors 3013 and 3241)

question: Can I test the log chain without a full restore?
answer: Partly. A chain integrity check confirms the LSN sequence is unbroken, which is a real and cheap check worth automating. It tells you point-in-time recovery is possible on paper, not that the files will read.
post_title: Restore Testing: Proving the Backups Actually Work

question: Do I need to test every database?
answer: No, and trying to is how the practice dies. Test the ones where recovery time is a commitment to somebody, plus a sample of the rest. A throughput figure from one large database tells you a lot about the others on the same storage.
post_title: Restore Testing: Proving the Backups Actually Work

question: Is RESTORE VERIFYONLY enough on its own?
answer: It is worth doing and it is not sufficient. It checks the backup set is readable and internally consistent; it does not read the pages of the database inside, so a backup of an already-corrupt database passes it. Pair it with regular CHECKDB on the source, and with a real restore periodically.
post_title: Restore Testing: Proving the Backups Actually Work

question: We use a third-party backup tool. Does that change anything?
answer: Not the argument. It changes the syntax and often adds its own verification step, which is still verification of the file rather than proof of recovery. The question "have we restored one" is the same question regardless of what wrote the file.
post_title: Restore Testing: Proving the Backups Actually Work

question: What if the restore fails?
answer: Then you have found the thing you were looking for, at a time when it costs you an afternoon rather than a business. Write down what failed, which is the point of keeping the numbers. Read the error above the closing message rather than the closing message itself, which is usually the least useful line in the output.
post_title: Restore Testing: Proving the Backups Actually Work

question: How do I see what the user really has, rather than what I think I granted?
answer: Ask SQL Server as that user. EXECUTE AS USER = 'name'; then SELECT permission_name FROM sys.fn_my_permissions('dbo.YourTable', 'OBJECT'); and REVERT;. This is worth more than reading role membership, because it resolves the whole chain for you. Adding a user to db_datareader and then putting an object-level DENY SELECT on one table returns Msg 229, Level 14, State 5 on that table and nothing back from fn_my_permissions, while the role membership still looks correct in every list you can read. A DENY anywhere beats a GRANT everywhere.
post_title: The SELECT Permission Was Denied on the Object (Error 229)

question: Should I just add db_datareader?
answer: If the genuine need is read-everything, yes, that is the honest fix and it survives object churn. If the need is one table, a role-wide grant is over-granting dressed up as convenience.
post_title: The SELECT Permission Was Denied on the Object (Error 229)

question: The user is in a role that has SELECT. Why still denied?
answer: A DENY somewhere wins over every GRANT, always. Check sys.database_permissions for DENY rows against the user AND every role it sits in; one hit is the whole answer.
post_title: The SELECT Permission Was Denied on the Object (Error 229)

question: Why did a view that worked for years suddenly throw this?
answer: An ownership chain broke. While view and table shared an owner, the table was never permission-checked through the view. A schema or ownership change ends that, and the caller suddenly needs rights on the base table.
post_title: The SELECT Permission Was Denied on the Object (Error 229)

question: I see 17113 and master.mdf in the log. Has the master database been lost?
answer: Probably not. 17113 says SQL Server could not open the file, not that the file is damaged, and the operating system error in brackets distinguishes them: 2 or 3 means it looked in the wrong place, 5 means it found the file and was refused. In the first case fix the -d parameter to point at where the file really is. In the second, fix the permissions on the folder. A genuinely unusable master gives you a different message, and Cannot Recover the Master Database (Error 3417) is that page.
post_title: SQL Server Service Will Not Start: Error 17113, 17058, 1067 and Where the Real Reason Is

question: Is this the same problem as SQL Server Agent not starting?
answer: No, and they need different fixes. This page is the database engine service. If the engine is running and it is the Agent that will not start, or the Agent node in Object Explorer is greyed out, that is a separate fault with its own error number, and SQL Server Agent Will Not Start covers it. The Agent cannot start while the engine is down, so if both are stopped, fix the engine first using this page and then check the Agent.
post_title: SQL Server Service Will Not Start: Error 17113, 17058, 1067 and Where the Real Reason Is

question: Should I rebuild master?
answer: Almost certainly not, and not until every path and permission on this page has been checked. MS Docs is clear on the cost in Rebuild system databases: master, model, msdb and tempdb are dropped and recreated, every user modification to them is lost, and all hotfixes have to be reapplied if the resource database goes with them. That means every login, every Agent job, every linked server and every server-level setting. Restoring master from backup is the better answer, and a wrong file path is not a reason to do either.
post_title: SQL Server Service Will Not Start: Error 17113, 17058, 1067 and Where the Real Reason Is

question: The SQL Server service won't start and all I get is error 1067. Where do I start?
answer: Not with 1067, because it carries no diagnosis. Read the last 20 lines of the ERRORLOG, which you can do with the service down and without a connection. If the log's last entry is older than your start attempt, go to the nothing-in-the-log section. MS Docs maps the Services applet wording for 1067 to a bad error log path, so that is the single most likely cause if the log itself tells you nothing, and the Windows Application log will carry the matching Event ID 17058 with the path in it.
post_title: SQL Server Service Will Not Start: Error 17113, 17058, 1067 and Where the Real Reason Is

question: The service started and then stopped. Is that different from not starting?
answer: Not usually. "Started and then stopped" is what the Services applet reports when the process launched and exited, which is the same thing 1067 describes, and the reason is in the ERRORLOG or on the console. The 1 case where it genuinely means something different is a start that reaches "SQL Server is now ready for client connections" and then shuts down later, which is not a startup problem at all: look for a shutdown request or a stack dump further down the same log, and check whether a cluster or an availability group resource is stopping the service on purpose.
post_title: SQL Server Service Will Not Start: Error 17113, 17058, 1067 and Where the Real Reason Is

question: What does "initerrlog: Could not open error log file" mean?
answer: It means the -e startup parameter points somewhere SQL Server cannot write, and it is error 17058. The operating system error in brackets tells you which half: 3 is the path does not exist, 5 is it does and the service account cannot write there. Because the error log is the thing it could not open, nothing about this fault appears in the error log, so read the Windows Application log instead, or run sqlservr in the foreground on Linux. The full section is here, including why the message repeats 10 times.
post_title: SQL Server Service Will Not Start: Error 17113, 17058, 1067 and Where the Real Reason Is

question: Where is the ERRORLOG if I cannot start the service to look it up?
answer: On disk, readable with any text editor, and it does not need SQL Server running. The defaults are <drive>:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\MSSQL.<n>\MSSQL\LOG\ERRORLOG on Windows and /var/opt/mssql/log/errorlog on Linux. If the instance was installed somewhere else, the -e parameter holds the real location, and on Windows you can read that from the registry under MSSQLServer\Parameters without opening Configuration Manager. The current log has no extension; ERRORLOG.1 is the previous start, which is the one you want if the service has since been restarted.
post_title: SQL Server Service Will Not Start: Error 17113, 17058, 1067 and Where the Real Reason Is

question: Can I fix it in the job step instead of changing the code?
answer: Yes, and it is often the quickest safe fix. Put the SET statements at the top of the T-SQL job step, before anything else runs. It is a per-connection setting, so it has to be set by whatever opens the connection.
post_title: SET Options Have Incorrect Settings (Error 1934)

question: Does this affect temporary tables and table variables?
answer: Only if they carry one of the features that demand the settings, which is unusual. The common case by far is a permanent table with a filtered index, added long after the code that writes to it.
post_title: SET Options Have Incorrect Settings (Error 1934)

question: Reads work, so is the index still being used?
answer: Yes, and that is the point of the split. Reading through the index does not change it, so no guarantee is needed. Writing has to update it, and if the session's options would change how the filter evaluates, the index could silently stop matching its own definition. Refusing the write is the safe behaviour.
post_title: SET Options Have Incorrect Settings (Error 1934)

question: Should I just drop the filtered index?
answer: That does clear the error, and it also throws away whatever the index was doing for you. Filtered indexes are usually there because someone measured a benefit. Fix the SET options first, and only revisit the index if it turns out nothing depends on it.
post_title: SET Options Have Incorrect Settings (Error 1934)

question: Which index is causing this?
answer: Look for a filtered index, an indexed view, or an index on a computed column on the table you are writing to. SELECT name, filter_definition FROM sys.indexes WHERE object_id = OBJECT_ID('dbo.YourTable') shows filtered indexes immediately, because filter_definition is only populated for them.
post_title: SET Options Have Incorrect Settings (Error 1934)

question: Why does it work in SSMS but not in my Agent job?
answer: Because they connect with different defaults. SSMS sets QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON; sqlcmd starts with it OFF, and older drivers vary. The code is identical, the session is not. Compare sys.dm_exec_sessions from both and the differing column is the answer.
post_title: SET Options Have Incorrect Settings (Error 1934)

question: Does any of this apply to Azure SQL Database?
answer: Some of it, differently. Backups and CHECKDB are managed for you there, so those entries fall away. Untrusted constraints, orphaned users, disabled indexes and stale statistics behave exactly the same, because they are properties of the database rather than of the instance. The audit script is written for SQL Server and reads instance-level catalogs, so it is not the tool to point at a single Azure SQL database.
post_title: Silent Failures: The SQL Server Problems That Never Raise an Error

question: How often should this run?
answer: Once when you take over an instance, then monthly. It is deliberately a slow-moving list: state drifts over months, not hours, and running it nightly would produce an unchanging report that people stop reading. If you want it scheduled, treat a new row appearing as the event worth alerting on rather than the report itself.
post_title: Silent Failures: The SQL Server Problems That Never Raise an Error

question: If these are so serious, why does SQL Server not warn about them?
answer: Because almost every one of them is a legitimate configuration that somebody chose. AUTO_SHRINK, TRUSTWORTHY, a job step that continues on failure and FULL recovery without log backups are all valid states with real use cases. A warning would be an opinion, and the engine does not hold opinions about how you run your estate. That is the correct design and it is also why the checking has to be yours. The instance can tell you what is true; only you can tell it what should be.
post_title: Silent Failures: The SQL Server Problems That Never Raise an Error

question: Is a green backup report really worth so little?
answer: It is worth exactly what it says: those backup operations completed. It is not a statement about recoverability, because nothing in the job asked whether the resulting chain restores. A FULL recovery model database with no log backups reports perfect coverage and gives you last night’s full backup and nothing since. The only real test is a restore. Everything short of that, including this script, is a way of narrowing down which servers to test first.
post_title: Silent Failures: The SQL Server Problems That Never Raise an Error

question: My constraint says it is enabled. Why does the script call it untrusted?
answer: Enabled and trusted are two different flags. WITH NOCHECK re-enables a constraint without validating the data already in the table, so SQL Server enforces it going forward but cannot promise the existing rows comply. Since it cannot promise, the optimizer will not use the constraint to simplify a plan. Re-validate with ALTER TABLE... WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT and the trust comes back.
post_title: Silent Failures: The SQL Server Problems That Never Raise an Error

question: Which one should I check first on a server I have just inherited?
answer: The backup chain, then integrity. Those two are the only entries on the list where the cost is unbounded: everything else degrades performance or widens a security surface, and both of those can lose data permanently. Run the audit, read the CRITICAL rows for Backups and Integrity, and deal with them before you look at anything else.
post_title: Silent Failures: The SQL Server Problems That Never Raise an Error

question: Does a SQL login get the same error, or is it only Windows accounts?
answer: Only Windows accounts, and that is the fastest test you have. SSPI is the Windows-authentication handshake, so it runs before SQL Server ever looks at a login. If a SQL authentication login connects to the same instance from the same machine at the same moment, the engine, the network path and the port are all fine, and the problem is Kerberos or the trust: an SPN, the service account, DNS, or the domain relationship. If the SQL login fails too, stop investigating SSPI and treat it as an ordinary connectivity or login failure.
post_title: SSPI Handshake Failed in SQL Server (Error 17806)

question: Does restarting SQL Server fix it?
answer: Occasionally, and misleadingly: a restart re-registers SPNs if the service account has permission to do so. If that is the fix, the real problem is SPN registration, and it will be back.
post_title: SSPI Handshake Failed in SQL Server (Error 17806)

question: Is "Cannot generate SSPI context" the same problem?
answer: Same family. That is the message the client typically sees while 17806 is the server error log side of the same failed negotiation, and the checklist is identical.
post_title: SSPI Handshake Failed in SQL Server (Error 17806)

question: It worked yesterday. What changes overnight?
answer: The classics: a VM clock drifting past the five-minute Kerberos tolerance, a machine password rotation breaking the secure channel, or a DNS change. All three are client-or-domain-side, which is why nothing on the SQL Server changed.
post_title: SSPI Handshake Failed in SQL Server (Error 17806)

question: Can I get the better message on an older version?
answer: Yes, on some. Trace flag 460 replaces Msg 8152 with Msg 2628 on SQL Server 2016 SP2 CU6, SQL Server 2017 CU12 and later, and it is still what turns the detailed message on for a database sitting at compatibility level 140 or lower on a newer instance. From compatibility level 150 the detailed message is the default and the flag has no effect. Confirmed on SQL Server 2025 CU8: with a database at compatibility level 130 the same insert returns Msg 8152, Level 16, State 30, and with trace flag 460 on it returns the full Msg 2628 instead. On anything older than those builds the practical answer is to narrow it down by comparing source and target column lengths.
post_title: Diagnose SQL Server’s ‘String or Binary Data Would Be Truncated’ Error

question: I am on a current version and still get the short message. Why?
answer: Check the database scoped configuration, not the compatibility level. VERBOSE_TRUNCATION_WARNINGS is ON by default, and with it turned OFF a database at compatibility level 170 goes straight back to Msg 8152, Level 16, State 30, with no table or column named. Measured both ways on SQL Server 2025 CU8. SELECT name, value FROM sys.database_scoped_configurations WHERE name = 'VERBOSE_TRUNCATION_WARNINGS' tells you which one you are on.
post_title: Diagnose SQL Server’s ‘String or Binary Data Would Be Truncated’ Error

question: Was anything written when the statement failed?
answer: No. Both messages end with The statement has been terminated, the statement is rolled back and the row is not inserted. The only time truncation writes anything is the silent case under SET ANSI_WARNINGS OFF, where the value is cut to fit and no error is raised at all.
post_title: Diagnose SQL Server’s ‘String or Binary Data Would Be Truncated’ Error

question: Which versions show the detailed Msg 2628?
answer: Any database at compatibility level 150 or higher, so SQL Server 2019 and later with a current compatibility level, where VERBOSE_TRUNCATION_WARNINGS is on by default. Below 150 you get Msg 8152 unless trace flag 460 is enabled, which needs SQL Server 2016 SP2 CU6 or SQL Server 2017 CU12 at minimum. Both facts are on the Microsoft pages linked above.
post_title: Diagnose SQL Server’s ‘String or Binary Data Would Be Truncated’ Error

question: Why does the old error not say which column?
answer: It was never designed to. Msg 8152 predates the improvement, and the reason it took so long is that naming the value risks putting data into an error message. Msg 2628 on 2019 and later does name it.
post_title: Diagnose SQL Server’s ‘String or Binary Data Would Be Truncated’ Error

question: Can users still read while the log is full?
answer: Yes. 9002 fails anything that has to write a log record, so inserts, updates, deletes and most DDL stop while SELECTs against committed data keep working. That is why the first sign is usually an application half working rather than an outage, and why nobody reports it until writes back up.
post_title: SQL Server Transaction Log Full

question: I took a log backup and log_reuse_wait_desc still says LOG_BACKUP.
answer: Two possibilities. The column reports what reuse was waiting on as of the last checkpoint, so it can lag behind what you just did: query it again and see if it clears. If it does not, check whether the backup was copy only, because a copy only log backup writes a perfectly valid file and truncates nothing. Reproduced on a test database: the value read LOG_BACKUP before, stayed LOG_BACKUP after BACKUP LOG... WITH COPY_ONLY, and only went to NOTHING after an ordinary log backup.
post_title: SQL Server Transaction Log Full

question: The log is full but log_reuse_wait_desc says NOTHING.
answer: Then nothing is holding the log open and the file simply cannot get any bigger. That is one of 3 things: autogrowth is off, the file has reached its configured max size, or the volume is out of space. Check the growth and max size settings on the log file before you go hunting for a blocking transaction that is not there.
post_title: SQL Server Transaction Log Full

question: The wait says ACTIVE_TRANSACTION but DBCC OPENTRAN returns nothing.
answer: The two are read at different moments. log_reuse_wait_desc reports the reason as of the last checkpoint, so a transaction that has since ended leaves a stale value behind while OPENTRAN, looking at the current state, correctly finds nothing. Re-check both. If the value persists with OPENTRAN still empty, look in sys.dm_tran_active_transactions for a prepared distributed transaction that never resolved.
post_title: SQL Server Transaction Log Full

question: Could antivirus be holding the file?
answer: Yes, and it usually shows as operating system error 32 rather than 5. Database files are a classic antivirus exclusion for this reason: the scanner opens the file, SQL Server cannot, and nothing in the SQL error message points at the scanner.
post_title: Unable to Open the Physical File (Error 5120)

question: Does this happen on restore as well as attach?
answer: Yes, and on startup. Anything that needs SQL Server to open a file on disk can raise it: attaching, restoring to a path it cannot write, or a database failing to come online after a volume changed. The operating system error still tells you which flavour you have.
post_title: Unable to Open the Physical File (Error 5120)

question: I granted Full Control and it still says access is denied.
answer: Then it is almost certainly not a permissions problem. The most common cause is that the file is already open, very often by this same SQL Server instance. Check sys.master_files for the physical path before changing anything else.
post_title: Unable to Open the Physical File (Error 5120)

question: The file is on a network share.
answer: That brings its own version of this. A virtual account has no identity off the machine, so a UNC path usually needs a domain service account and the share permissions to match. Local storage is the simpler answer where you have the choice.
post_title: Unable to Open the Physical File (Error 5120)

question: Which account do I actually grant to?
answer: Whatever sys.dm_server_services reports, which on a default modern install is a virtual account like NT Service\MSSQLSERVER rather than a domain user. Grant on the folder with inheritance, so files added later are covered too.
post_title: Unable to Open the Physical File (Error 5120)

question: Why does my error handler only show 1802?
answer: Because 1802 is the terminating error for the statement and 5120 is a related error raised alongside it. Verified on SQL Server 2025: ERROR_NUMBER() returned 1802 for a missing file, a file in use, and a file with no permission. Read the error log for the 5120.
post_title: Unable to Open the Physical File (Error 5120)

question: Can I upgrade and move hardware at once?
answer: That is exactly what side-by-side is. One window, one validation, and a rollback that does not involve a restore.
post_title: SQL Server Version Upgrade Runbook: Side-by-Side and In-Place

question: Should I raise compatibility level immediately?
answer: Raise it deliberately and test it, but do not leave it indefinitely. A database sitting two versions behind its host is a decision nobody made, and it gets harder to change the longer it sits there.
post_title: SQL Server Version Upgrade Runbook: Side-by-Side and In-Place

question: What changes most noticeably after an upgrade?
answer: Query plans, through the cardinality estimator. This is why a performance baseline taken before the upgrade is worth more than any amount of reassurance afterwards.
post_title: SQL Server Version Upgrade Runbook: Side-by-Side and In-Place

question: Which upgrade path is supported directly?
answer: It depends on both ends, and the runbook lists the matrix. The assessment flags whether your specific source-to-target path is direct or needs a hop, which is better than finding out from setup.exe.
post_title: SQL Server Version Upgrade Runbook: Side-by-Side and In-Place

question: Can I just run the DMV twice by hand instead of a collector job?
answer: Yes, and for a one-off investigation that is the sensible thing to do: select the counters into a temp table, wait, select again, join on wait type and subtract. The collector job earns its place when you want the window that has already passed, which is most of the time, because incidents are usually reported after they end.
post_title: Cumulative Wait Stats Lie: Measuring Waits Over an Interval

question: Does the delta approach work across a failover?
answer: No, and for the same reason as a restart. The replica you are now reading has its own counters that started when it came up, so the earlier snapshot belongs to a different instance. Treat a failover as a reset.
post_title: Cumulative Wait Stats Lie: Measuring Waits Over an Interval

question: How long should the interval be?
answer: Long enough to contain the behaviour you are chasing and short enough to exclude everything else. Fifteen minutes to an hour suits most investigations. A five-minute window during a live incident is more useful than a daily average; a daily average is more useful for capacity questions than a five-minute window.
post_title: Cumulative Wait Stats Lie: Measuring Waits Over an Interval

question: Should I still look at the cumulative numbers at all?
answer: They are useful for one thing: a long-run profile of what the server spends its life waiting on. Just do not use them to diagnose something that started on Tuesday.
post_title: Cumulative Wait Stats Lie: Measuring Waits Over an Interval

question: Why is my top wait something I have never heard of?
answer: Many wait types are internal housekeeping that a healthy instance accumulates constantly and nobody should chase. That is what the wait library is for: look the type up before acting on it, because "top of the list" and "worth investigating" are not the same claim.
post_title: Cumulative Wait Stats Lie: Measuring Waits Over an Interval

question: Are contained users a security risk?
answer: They shift where the risk sits rather than adding to it. Password policy for a contained user is enforced by the host Windows policy of whichever instance the database is attached to, so moving the database can move the policy. More importantly, anyone with ALTER ANY USER in a contained database can create an account that connects to that database, without going anywhere near a server administrator. That is the whole feature, and it is a real delegation of authority worth making deliberately.
post_title: CREATE USER WITHOUT LOGIN vs Contained Database Users

question: Can I convert a WITHOUT LOGIN user into a real one?
answer: Yes, in both directions, with ALTER USER. ALTER USER [x] WITH LOGIN = [SomeLogin] binds it to a server login, and in a contained database ALTER USER [x] WITH PASSWORD gives it its own password. Be deliberate about it though: converting a WITHOUT LOGIN user that exists purely for EXECUTE AS into something connectable hands out a login-capable account carrying whatever permissions that impersonation identity was granted.
post_title: CREATE USER WITHOUT LOGIN vs Contained Database Users

question: Do contained users work without CONTAINMENT = PARTIAL?
answer: No. You need two things: the instance option contained database authentication set to 1, and the database itself set to CONTAINMENT = PARTIAL. Without both, CREATE USER... WITH PASSWORD fails outright. This is worth knowing before a migration, because the target database has to be configured the same way before you can recreate the user at all.
post_title: CREATE USER WITHOUT LOGIN vs Contained Database Users

question: Does a WITHOUT LOGIN user have a SID?
answer: It does, and that surprises people. SQL Server generates one so the principal can own objects and hold permissions like any other. It just does not correspond to any server login, which is exactly why a tool that matches users to logins by SID finds nothing and has to decide what that means. Deciding it means “script it as WITHOUT LOGIN” is right for this user and wrong for a contained one.
